true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize silently replaces the width/height version

The file now defines self.downsize twice: at line 145 as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) and again at line 149 as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}). In Ruby the last definition wins, so the width/height version at line 145 is dead code, and any existing caller (including specs) that invokes OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height) will now raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments, 5 for 3..4) at runtime. Keep a single signature: either delete the width/height variant, or have it build the dimensions string and delegate to the new one.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check hardcodes 10 MB and ignores max_image_size_kb / max_attachment_size_kb

validateUploadedFile used to check file size against Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']; it now uses a hardcoded 10 * 1024 for every upload type. This breaks the attachment path: a forum with max_attachment_size_kb set above 10 MB (e.g. to allow zips or videos) now has legitimate uploads rejected in the browser, and a forum with a lower attachment limit lets oversized files through only to fail on the server after the upload. For images it also ignores the configured limit in both directions — sites that raised max_image_size_kb above 10 MB still block larger images client-side — and the file_too_large message always reports 10 MB regardless of the actual setting. The per-type site settings should remain the source of truth, with any extra headroom for server-side downsizing applied only to type 'image'.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Downsize loop reads size from a stale file handle and ignores downsize failures

The loop condition `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` uses Tempfile#size, which is fstat() on the already-open file handle. OptimizedImage.downsize -> convert_with runs ImageOptim.optimize_image!, which — when it improves the image (the common case) — replaces the file at tempfile.path by moving a newly written file over it, i.e. a new inode. The open handle keeps pointing at the old, unlinked inode, so tempfile.size stays frozen at the size captured after the first convert and never reflects further reductions. Consequences: (1) an image that needs more than one pass to get under the limit is downsized all 5 times — shrunk to 0.8^5 ≈ 33% of its dimensions and lossily recompressed/optimized five times, degrading quality and burning CPU; (2) the same stale tempfile.size is passed to Upload.create_for on line 72, so an image that was actually reduced below the limit can be stored with, and validated against, its old larger filesize and still be rejected. The loop also ignores OptimizedImage.downsize's return value, so a failing convert is retried identically five times. Check File.size(tempfile.path), pass that value to create_for, and break out of the loop when downsize returns false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message now always claims the upload limit is 10 MB

The 413 (entity too large) handler in displayErrorForUpload used to report Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb in the file_too_large message; it now hardcodes 10 * 1024. Whenever the site's configured limit, or the web server's actual body-size limit that produced the 413, differs from 10 MB, the user is shown the wrong maximum size. The message should use the site setting or the real configured limit.

API URL-download size cap hardcoded to 10 MB instead of max_image_size_kb

FileHelper.download for URL-based API uploads is now called with 10.megabytes rather than SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes. On sites where the admin raised the image size limit above 10 MB, downloads that used to succeed now exceed the hardcoded cap; FileHelper.download raises, the rescue sets tempfile to nil, and the code then hits the pre-existing nil-tempfile path (tempfile.size at line 72 raises NoMethodError), turning a previously valid upload into a 500. The cap should stay tied to the site setting (or a single shared constant) instead of a magic number that can drift from configuration.

No tests for the auto-downsize upload path

This PR adds a server-side resize loop to UploadsController#create_upload and changes OptimizedImage.downsize's signature, but no specs were added or updated (only these three files changed). There is no coverage for: an oversized image being downsized below max_image_size_kb and accepted, termination when the image cannot be reduced enough, the animated-GIF branch, or the new downsize signature. Given the subtleties involved (the downsize tool replacing the file vs. the open tempfile handle, and the duplicate method definition in optimized_image.rb), controller and model specs should be added before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation raises NoMethodError when host is nil

The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. If a record is built without a host (for example an admin API request missing `embeddable_host[host]`, which `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host` assigns without a presence check), `sub!` is invoked on nil and raises NoMethodError, turning what should be a validation failure into a 500. Guard with `if self.host.present?` (or use non-mutating `sub` after a nil check) and add `validates_presence_of :host`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update and destroy 500 on an unknown host id instead of returning 404

`update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and passes the result to `save_host`, which immediately calls `host.host = ...`; `destroy` calls `host.destroy`. If the id does not exist (stale page, deleted host, scripted request), `host` is nil and both actions raise NoMethodError, returning a 500. Other admin controllers in the codebase handle this by raising Discourse::NotFound (404); these actions should do the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy host values are inserted raw and may silently stop matching after migration

The migration copies values from the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting straight into the new table with `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, ...) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. The old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` stripped `http(s)://` prefixes when matching (and the old specs explicitly covered scheme-prefixed entries working), but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares the bare hostname (`uri.host`) against the stored value with `lower(host) = ?`. The model strips schemes/paths in `before_validation`, but the migration bypasses the model, so any legacy entries stored as `http://example.com`, with paths, uppercase, or trailing `\r` from Windows line endings will be inserted verbatim and will never match again — embedding silently breaks for those sites. Additionally the value is interpolated directly into the SQL string, so a host containing a single quote produces invalid SQL and fails the migration; values should be normalized and passed through quoting/bound parameters.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents were swapped

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now contains `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the category fabricators (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) were moved into `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The suite still loads because Fabrication reads every file in the directory, but the fabricators live in files with the wrong names, which will confuse future maintainers; the contents should be swapped so each fabricator lives in its namesake file.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy host values are inserted raw and may silently stop matching after migration

The migration copies values from the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting straight into the new table with `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, ...) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. The old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` stripped `http(s)://` prefixes when matching (and the old specs explicitly covered scheme-prefixed entries working), but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares the bare hostname (`uri.host`) against the stored value with `lower(host) = ?`. The model strips schemes/paths in `before_validation`, but the migration bypasses the model, so any legacy entries stored as `http://example.com`, with paths, uppercase, or trailing `\r` from Windows line endings will be inserted verbatim and will never match again — embedding silently breaks for those sites. Additionally the value is interpolated directly into the SQL string, so a host containing a single quote produces invalid SQL and fails the migration; values should be normalized and passed through quoting/bound parameters.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the embed_category site setting row is missing or unmatched

The migration computes the default category with `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. site_settings only contains rows for settings an admin explicitly changed, and `embed_category` defaulted to blank, so for the vast majority of installations (and every fresh install) this query returns zero rows. Indexing `[0]` on an empty result set returns nil (or raises IndexError depending on the pg adapter version), so `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError and the entire migration aborts, blocking the upgrade. The fallback for `category_id == 0` on line 15 (`... WHERE name = 'uncategorized_category_id'")[0]['value']`) has the same problem if that row is absent. Both lookups need to tolerate an empty result (e.g. `.first` with a nil check or a begin/rescue) before dereferencing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

false_positives.candidate:
Host regex rejects valid TLDs longer than 5 characters

The TLD portion of the validation regex is `[a-z]{2,5}`, which rejects real domains under longer TLDs such as `.museum`, `.travel`, or `.technology`. The previous free-form site setting accepted these hosts, so sites embedding from such domains can no longer add them through the new admin UI. The TLD segment should allow a more generous length (e.g. `{2,}`).

Host validation accepts ports but record lookup can never match them

The validation regex `/\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` explicitly permits an optional `:port` suffix, so an admin can successfully save `example.com:3000`. However `record_for_host` compares `uri.host` — which never includes the port — against the stored value, so a host saved with a port will never match and embedding from it will always be rejected. Either strip the port in `before_validation` like the scheme/path are stripped, or disallow it in the regex.

New admin controllers have no request-level specs

Both new controller specs (`admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb`) only assert that the controller is a subclass of Admin::AdminController. There is no coverage for create/update/destroy behavior, validation errors, the category defaulting to uncategorized, or the unknown-id case — which is how the nil-host NoMethodError in `update`/`destroy` slips through. At minimum, request specs exercising the happy paths and the missing-record paths should be added.

New host saved without choosing a category shows a blank category until reload

In the `save` action, after the record is created the component runs `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))`. For a newly added host the `categoryId` property starts as null (the user is not required to pick a category; the server substitutes `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id`), so `findById(null)` returns undefined and the row's category badge renders blank even though the server assigned the uncategorized category. The correct category only appears after a full page reload. The component should resolve the category from the category_id returned in the save response when `categoryId` is unset.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser row

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` returns nil whenever the user has no topic_users row for that topic (e.g., they never visited or interacted with it, or the row was removed). The very next line dereferences `tu.notification_level`, so such a request raises NoMethodError and returns a 500. This endpoint is the target of links sent in notification emails, so it must be robust for any logged-in user. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`, which creates the row when missing, or explicitly handle the nil case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
No request/controller spec for the new state-changing unsubscribe endpoint

This PR adds a new public, state-changing endpoint (TopicsController#unsubscribe) but only touches spec/components/email/message_builder_spec.rb to pass the new unsubscribe_url option. There is no controller/request spec covering the unsubscribe action itself: the slug redirect behavior, the watching/tracking -> regular and regular -> muted transitions, and the no-existing-TopicUser-row case (which currently 500s). A spec would have caught the nil dereference before merge.

unsubscribe mutates notification state via an unauthenticated-format GET request The new unsubscribe endpoint is routed as GET (`get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb) and is added to `skip_before_filter :check_xhr`, and it immediately changes `TopicUser.notification_level` (`tu.save!`) when the URL is fetched. Rails' CSRF protection does not cover GET requests, so the only guard is the session cookie: anyone can change a logged-in victim's topic notification state (mute the topic, or demote it from watching/tracking to regular) by getting their browser to request the URL, e.g. by embedding `` in a post, PM, or external page. It also violates safe-GET semantics, so browser prefetchers can trigger it. The mutation should require a POST (the unsubscribe page already renders a notification control that could perform it), or at minimum a confirmation step.

unsubscribe saves TopicUser directly, bypassing TopicUser.change side effects

Everywhere else in the app, notification level changes go through `TopicUser.change`, which also sets `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` (so the UI can explain why the level is what it is) and publishes a `notification_level_change` MessageBus event so the user's other open tabs/sessions update live. The new unsubscribe action instead assigns `tu.notification_level` and calls `tu.save!`, so those timestamps/reason stay stale and other browser sessions never learn the topic was muted. Calling `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: level)` would fix this and the nil-row crash in the same action.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validator performs DB writes during validation; match_count is double-counted per signup

validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which as a side effect increments match_count and sets last_match_at on the blocked_emails row. Validation is normally read-only, and here it runs more than once per signup: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` at line 168 (before the DiscourseHub check) and then `user.save` at line 172, which validates again — so one blocked signup attempt records two matches. Any other `user.valid?`/`save` with a changed email (including records that fail for unrelated reasons or are rolled back) also bumps the counters, so match_count cannot be trusted as a count of signup attempts. The stats update should happen once, at the point the signup is actually rejected, not inside the validator.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive, so blocks are trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact `where(email: email)` lookup, and the signup flow stores emails exactly as typed: `User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` raw, the User model has no email downcasing callback, and the email uniqueness validator plus the Postgres unique index on users.email are both case-sensitive. Blocking `spammer@example.com` therefore does nothing to stop `Spammer@example.com` or `SPAMMER@example.com` from registering — the lookup misses the row and a separate account is created. The block should normalize case (store emails lowercase and compare against `email.downcase`) to be effective as an anti-abuse control.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the new errors/values response contract the client depends on

The failed-signup JSON now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, and the new client behavior — pushing `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` only when `result.errors.email` is present — depends on both keys existing with exactly these shapes. No controller/request spec (or JS test) was added for this contract, so a rename or a change in how errors are serialized would silently break the "prevent resubmitting a blocked email" flow without any failing test.

match_count increment is a read-modify-write and loses updates under concurrency

In BlockedEmail.should_block?, `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both read the same value, so one increment is silently lost. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")` or `update_counters`, which also avoids re-running validations and callbacks for a stats update.

rejectedEmails array is defined on the prototype and shared across instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` in the hash passed to `Discourse.Controller.extend` puts a single mutable array on the controller's prototype, shared by every instance. The app currently instantiates this controller once, but any second instantiation — in JS tests, or if the controller is torn down and recreated — inherits emails rejected during earlier usage, and mutations via `pushObject` leak between instances. Initialize it per-instance instead, e.g. in an `init()` override with `this.set('rejectedEmails', Em.A([]))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is the full referer URL — browsers throw and the iframe never resizes

The layout calls parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: ...}, '<%= request.referer %>'). The referer is a full URL with a path (e.g. http://blog.example.com/2013/02/post.html), but targetOrigin must be an origin (scheme://host[:port]); Chrome/Firefox throw a SyntaxError ('Invalid target origin') for anything else. As a result the discourse-resize message is never delivered to the parent page and the embed.js auto-resize feature simply never works. The code should post to the referer's origin only. Additionally, the referer is interpolated into a single-quoted JS string and html_escape does not escape apostrophes on all Rails versions this repo supports, so a referer containing a raw ' would also break the script.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feeds without content:encoded crash the hourly job (nil.scrub)

For RSS 2.0 feeds that don't provide <content:encoded> — many feeds only ship <description> — SimpleRSS returns nil for i.content, so `i.content.scrub` raises NoMethodError. The hourly PollFeed job dies partway through the feed and all remaining items are skipped every run. Use a fallback such as (i.content || i.description) and guard for nil before calling scrub.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

postMessage targetOrigin is the full referer URL — browsers throw and the iframe never resizes

The layout calls parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: ...}, '<%= request.referer %>'). As a result the discourse-resize message is never delivered to the parent page and the embed.js auto-resize feature simply never works. The code should post to the referer's origin only. Additionally, the referer is interpolated into a single-quoted JS string and html_escape does not escape apostrophes on all Rails versions this repo supports, so a referer containing a raw ' would also break the script.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate:
ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT + NOT NULL rewrites the entire posts table and blocks writes

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false forces PostgreSQL (< 11) to rewrite every row of the posts table while holding an AccessExclusiveLock. posts is the largest table in a Discourse install, so on any sizable forum this migration blocks all posting/reading for minutes during a deploy. Safer pattern: add the column without a default, backfill in batches, then set the default and the NOT NULL constraint.

Editing an already-released migration and adding force: true

This changes the shipped 20131223171005_create_top_topics migration to create_table :top_topics, force: true. Databases that already ran the migration will never re-run it, so the change is a silent no-op there; on fresh or restored setups, force: true will silently DROP and recreate the table (and any data) if it already exists. Released migrations shouldn't be modified — add a new migration instead. The new db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb uses force: true too, carrying the same silent-drop risk.

Find-then-create race on embed_url unique index aborts concurrent import jobs

import does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and later TopicEmbed.create! inside a transaction. Two concurrent jobs for the same URL (a RetrieveTopic job racing the hourly PollFeed, or two RetrieveTopic jobs for staff, who bypass the redis throttle) both see no existing embed and both build a topic and post; the second create! hits the unique index on topic_embeds.embed_url and raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, failing that job — and in PollFeed, aborting the rest of the feed items. Rescue RecordNotUnique/re-check inside the transaction or use an upsert-style create_or_find.

Gating tests for feed_polling_url / embed_by_username are vacuous

The tests 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' never enable the preceding conditions: feed_polling_enabled? defaults to false in the test env (and the URL is unset in the username test), so execute short-circuits at the first condition and `poller.expects(:poll_feed).never` passes regardless of the condition under test. These specs would still pass if the url/username presence checks were removed entirely. Each gating test should stub all the prior conditions to true so only the condition under test fails.

Loading page self-reload fails the controller's referer check — embed gets stuck on 403

The loading page reloads itself every 30s via document.location.reload() so it picks up the topic once the RetrieveTopic job finishes. A programmatic reload sends the iframe's own URL (the /embed/best URL on the forum host) as the Referer, not the embedding page's URL. EmbedController#ensure_embeddable (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:26) compares URI(referer).host to SiteSetting.embeddable_host and raises Discourse::InvalidAccess on mismatch, so the reload gets a 403 and the embed is permanently stuck on an error page instead of showing the newly imported topic. The referer check needs to also accept the forum's own embed URL (or the loading flow needs another mechanism, e.g. message-bus).

Non-atomic setnx + expire can permanently throttle an embed URL

retrieved_recently? does $redis.setnx(retrieved_key, '1') followed by a separate $redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60). If the process crashes (or expire raises) between the two calls, the key never expires and retrieve() will treat that embed_url as recently retrieved forever — the topic is never fetched. Use a single atomic SET with an EX option (supported by redis-rb) instead of the two-step dance.

RSS feed content is stored as raw, unsanitized HTML — stored XSS on the forum domain

PollFeed takes each feed item's HTML (CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)) and passes it to TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html] (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22). Post#cook returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html posts (app/models/post.rb:133), so `cooked` contains the feed markup verbatim with zero sanitization, and it is rendered unescaped (<%= raw post.cooked %> in app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19, and as cooked HTML in the main app). Any <script> or on* handler in a feed item becomes stored XSS executing on the forum domain for every visitor. The CGI.unescapeHTML makes this worse: the XML parser already decodes entities once, so content the feed author properly escaped (e.g. `<script>` in a code sample) is decoded a second time into live markup — even a fully trusted blog can inject live scripts. Note the import_remote path at least whitelists tags/attributes via Readability; the RSS path sanitizes nothing. Feed content should be run through Sanitize (or an equivalent whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

Server-side fetch follows redirects to any host — SSRF past the embeddable_host check

TopicRetriever#invalid_host? only validates that URI(embed_url).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but TopicEmbed.import_remote fetches with `open(url)` (open-uri), which transparently follows HTTP redirects to arbitrary hosts. An open redirect on the allowed host (e.g. http://blog.example.com/out?u=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data or an intranet address) lets an external requester make the forum server fetch internal URLs; the response is then Readability-parsed and published as a public topic, exfiltrating the content. The fetch layer should validate every redirect target against the allowed host or disable cross-host redirects.

URIs that pass the regex but are invalid crash the whole import run

Even if the key type were fixed, value_from_cursor would need to convert the millisecond cursor value back to a datetime (as DateTimePaginator does); as written the integer is compared directly against a timestamp column, which Postgres rejects. true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member.has_global_access crashes when member is None

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated on every GET to this endpoint, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `organization_context.member` is `None` for requests authenticated without an organization membership (e.g. org auth tokens or API keys carrying org:admin scope), and for any non-superuser such request the attribute access raises AttributeError, turning previously working requests into 500s. Guard for None (e.g. `member = organization_context.member; enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or (member is not None and member.has_global_access)`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

false_positives.candidate:
Redirect-chain limit lowered from 10000 to 1000; over-limit chains silently mis-join segments

The redirect resolution loop now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000. When the limit is hit the loop simply ends with `set_span_id` pointing at a mid-chain span, and the incoming span is merged into that mid-chain set (recreating an unlinked key as a new orphan segment) rather than the segment root — fragmenting the segment into separately flushed pieces. Redirect entries persist for `redis_ttl` (1h) for every span id ever seen, independent of the new 1000-span payload cap, so very active traces can still build chains longer than 1000. If the lower bound is intentional, at least log or metric when the loop exits without resolving (redirect_depth == 1000) so the fragmentation is observable.

Set→sorted-set change will WRONGTYPE-fail on segment keys written before the deploy

Segment keys (`span-buf:s:*`) were previously plain Redis sets written with SADD; this PR switches all access to sorted-set commands (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). Existing keys live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), so after a rolling deploy, any batch or flush touching a pre-deploy key raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` — the Lua EVALSHA aborts and `p.execute()` raises, failing the whole Kafka batch until those keys expire or are flushed. There is no migration step or type-tolerant handling; this needs an explicit rollout plan (flush the buffer cluster, or drain before enabling).

ZUNIONSTORE default AGGREGATE SUM doubles scores of duplicated spans, skewing eviction

`zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` uses Redis's default AGGREGATE SUM, so when the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a duplicate/redelivered span that was previously merged), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps — roughly 2× the real time. Since eviction is `zpopmin` (lowest score first), such a duplicated span is artificially protected from eviction and will survive while genuinely newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so duplicated members keep a sane score.

end_timestamp_precise is used as a Redis score without validation; one bad span fails the whole batch

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is passed straight through as the ZADD score for the span payload. `rapidjson.loads` accepts NaN/Infinity, and Redis rejects non-finite ZADD scores with an error, so a single malformed span makes the entire `p.execute()` pipeline fail — failing and reprocessing the whole Kafka batch rather than just the bad span. Previously the payload went into a plain set so this value was never interpreted. Sanitize the score (e.g. skip or clamp non-finite values) before building the ZADD mapping.

max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; the only enforcement is a hardcoded 1000 in Lua

The Python-side guard in `_load_segment_data` that skipped segments exceeding `self.max_segment_spans` (and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) was deleted, but `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001). The only remaining enforcement is the hardcoded `if span_count > 1000` in add-buffer.lua, which neither matches the default (1001) nor any configured value — anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` now gets a silent no-op, and the span-count cap diverges from the documented setting. Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or remove the parameter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses built-in hash() of project ids; invalidation helper is dead code

The eligibility cache key is built with Python's `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Using `hash()` for a cache key is fragile: two different project-id sets in the same organization that collide would share an eligibility decision for 60 seconds, silently applying (or withholding) upsampling for the wrong project set and returning wrong counts. Use an explicit, collision-free key (e.g. the joined sorted ids). Relatedly, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called from anywhere in the codebase, so despite its docstring ('should be called when the allowlist configuration changes') nothing invalidates on option changes — and the docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` ('reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time') now contradicts the 60-second caching layered on top of it, which is misleading for the next person touching this code.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is checked against the request-level dataset/query instead of the scoped dataset/query actually executed

Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over `dataset` and `request` from `get()`, but `_get_event_stats` is invoked with a `scoped_dataset` and a possibly rewritten `query` argument. In the dashboard discover-split flow (`metrics_enhanced and dashboard_widget_id`), the error branch calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction", ...)`: here `dataset` is still `metrics_performance`/`metrics_enhanced_performance`, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False and the error split query is never upsampled — while the same projects queried via the errors/discover dataset would return upsampled counts, giving inconsistent numbers for allowlisted orgs depending on which path served the widget. Similarly, `_is_error_focused_query` reads `request.GET['query']`, so it never sees the augmented `!event.type:transaction` / `event.type:transaction` split queries and can misclassify them. The eligibility check should be based on `scoped_dataset` and the `query` parameter passed into `_get_event_stats`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental nested git submodule (gitlink) committed

This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d2909...`, i.e. a gitlink pinning a nested checkout of the sentry repository itself (at this PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is almost certainly an accidental artifact of having a local clone inside the working tree. Once merged, every checkout of the repo will contain an uninitializable submodule directory, `git status` will permanently show it, and CI/checkout tooling that recurses or validates submodules may fail. It should be removed from the PR.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring matching on the raw query string, producing false positives

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET['query']` and checks `'event.type:error' in query`. This is not a parsed search match: a query like `message:"saw event.type:error in logs"` or a longer value such as `event.type:errortag` contains the substring and will be classified as error-focused. The `count()` → `sum(sample_weight)` transform is then applied to a query that also matches transactions/other events, whose `sample_weight` is NULL, so those events are counted as 0 and the returned counts are wrong. If the intent is to only transform queries that filter to error events, the query should be parsed (or at minimum token-boundary matched) rather than substring-matched.

upsampled_count registered without private=True, exposing an internal-only function in the public query API

The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` does not set `private=True`, unlike the sibling internal helper directly above it in `function_converter`. Public functions are selectable by any API user in arbitrary discover/events queries (`upsampled_count()` in `field`/`yAxis`) and may surface in docs/function-listing surfaces. Since this function is an implementation detail of the error-upsampling feature (injected by the endpoint itself, which works regardless of visibility) and returns misleading values on non-allowlisted or unsampled data, it should be marked `private=True` to keep it out of the public query surface.

upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no NULL fallback, silently dropping unsampled errors

The new `upsampled_count()` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum()` skips NULL values, so any error event whose `sample_weight` is NULL contributes 0 to the count. NULL weights occur for events ingested before the project was allowlisted / before the column existed, and for events the SDK/Relay sent without an `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` context (e.g. projects at sample rate 1.0 that never attach the context). The code comments assert 'sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects', but nothing enforces this: the allowlist is a mutable option applied to projects with pre-existing data. Consequence: for allowlisted projects, `count()` becomes an undercount that silently excludes exactly those events, which is worse than not upsampling at all. The aggregate should coalesce missing weights, e.g. `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, toFloat64(1)))` (or `ifNull(sample_weight, 1)`), so unsampled events count once. Note the new snuba tests only store events that carry the `error_sampling` context, so this failure mode is not covered anywhere.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs error_ids with nodestore results positionally, which is not order-safe

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, and then builds events via `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id and does not guarantee that `.values()` comes back in the same order as the requested `node_ids` (and missing keys may be omitted or set to `None`, shifting subsequent pairs). As a result, the `id` recorded on each `ErrorEvent` can be paired with a different event's data. Today the downstream log generation only reads `title`/`message`/`timestamp` (which come from the same data object), so the user-facing impact is currently limited to the latent `id` field being wrong, but the pairing should be done by iterating the node ids and looking up `events[node_id]` instead of relying on positional zip.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization path renders a hardcoded empty table

In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` organization feature is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with completely hardcoded empty data instead of the actual `result.data`/`result.meta` from the query. The flagged branch also ignores `loading` (no placeholder while loading), errors, `title`, and the `getCustomFieldRenderer`/`fieldHeaderMap` wiring that the existing `StyledSimpleTableChart` path uses. The moment anyone enables this flag for an organization, every table-type dashboard widget will render an empty table with zero columns and no loading state, silently hiding all data. Either wire the real `tableResults` data through or don't merge the flag check until the visualization actually consumes query results.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

false_positives.candidate:
HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only filtered when a search query is present

The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES = ['is_segment', 'project_id', 'received']` list is applied inside the memo like this: `if (!searchQuery.trim()) { return sorted; }` followed by `sorted.filter(attribute => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name) && ...)`. Because the early return happens for the empty-search case, the hidden attributes are only excluded while the user is actively typing a search query. In the default attribute view (no search entered), `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are still rendered, which defeats the purpose of the hidden list. The `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` predicate should be applied to `sorted` regardless of whether a search query is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code redemption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The login flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then writes the updated array back in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent sign-in requests presenting the same backup code can both decrypt and pass `indexOf` before either update commits, so a code intended to be single-use can be redeemed twice. Use a transaction with a conditional update (or a per-code consumed flag updated atomically) so only one request can consume a given code.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login can skip password verification entirely

In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password check at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the new backup-code branch at line 131 verifies only the backup code. A crafted request to the credentials callback containing a valid `backupCode` together with any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips `verifyPassword` and is authenticated solely by the backup code — a static, 40-bit secret that users store in files/notes. Backup codes are meant to substitute for the authenticator as the second factor, not to replace the password, so a leaked backup code alone yields full account access. The password should be verified (when the user has one) before accepting a backup code, or the flow branching should be keyed off the presence of `backupCode` instead of piggybacking on the `totpCode` gate.

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashing

Backup codes are stored via `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`. Unlike the TOTP secret, the stored codes are never read back for display — the one-time display uses the in-memory values returned by this same endpoint, and login/disable only need an equality check — so they could be stored as one-way hashes (like passwords). As implemented, anyone who obtains both the database and the encryption key recovers every user's unused backup codes in cleartext.

Backup codes unusable in the SAML/Google TOTP login flow

When a user with 2FA logs in via Google/SAML they are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` (`totpEmail` set), and in that state the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only offers Cancel — there is no "Lost access" option, so these users cannot enter a backup code even though the credentials provider would accept one. Accounts that enabled 2FA and later moved to an identity-provider login (e.g. after linking Google, which nulls the password) have no self-service recovery path if they lose their authenticator.

Consumed backup codes are nulled instead of removed

After a successful redemption the code does `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts the array, so the stored value permanently accumulates null placeholders (e.g. `[null, null, "abc123...", ...]`). Single-use still works because `indexOf` no longer matches the redeemed string, but the stored blob grows with junk entries and reveals exactly how many codes have been used. Splice the element out (or filter nulls) before re-encrypting.

Copy button shows a success toast even when the clipboard write fails

The copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without awaiting or catching it, then immediately fires `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")`. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied, `writeText` rejects (an unhandled promise rejection) while the user is told the codes were copied — they may close the dialog believing they have codes they don't. Await the promise and only show the success toast on fulfillment, with an error toast on rejection.

Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step loses the codes with no recovery path

The backup codes are shown exactly once on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step, and only the explicit Close button calls `onEnable()`. If the user dismisses the dialog at this step in any other way (ESC key or the dialog's close control, which fire `onOpenChange`), the modal closes without `onEnable` being called and the codes — which exist only in this component's React state — can never be displayed or regenerated again. The user's only recourse is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Consider intercepting dismissal on this step with a warning, or providing a way to regenerate codes later.

No test exercises the actual backup-code authentication behavior

The only test additions assert that the download/copy/close buttons render on the post-enable screen. Nothing tests the security-critical behavior of the feature: logging in with a backup code, that a redeemed code is invalidated and cannot be reused, that the password is still required alongside a backup code (see the related finding on password skipping), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The added TODO comment ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the unchecked PR checklist item concede this. For an authentication feature, the login-with-backup-code and single-use-invalidation paths should be covered before merge.

Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from keyboard navigation in every `PasswordField` across the app, while it keeps only an sr-only label. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reach the control to verify what they typed. If the goal was to streamline tab order, this trades away an accessibility affordance; consider leaving it focusable.

missing_backup_codes message directs users to a settings option that does not exist

The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes outside the initial 2FA setup. Every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped has `backupCodes = null`; if they lose their authenticator and use the new "Lost access" link at login, they hit `MissingBackupCodes` and are told to do something impossible — they cannot log in to reach settings, and even in settings there is no regeneration option. These users are effectively locked out (admin intervention required). Either add a regeneration flow or change the message.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent fallback find compares against a known-falsy externalCalendarId

`const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;` — in the fallback branch `externalCalendarId` is falsy by definition, so the `find` predicate compares each calendar's externalId against null/undefined/'' and effectively never matches, yielding `calendarId: undefined` for the update call. The old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Bookings whose reference lacks `externalCalendarId` (legacy rows) will now attempt to update `calendars/undefined/events/...` and fail, whereas before they updated the destination calendar. The same dead predicate exists in `deleteEvent` (line ~317), where it silently degrades to deleting from "primary" instead of the destination calendar.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated change inverts organization slug logic for team billing

This PR flips `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` while keeping `requestedSlug` also set when billing is enabled. Previously, when team billing was enabled the org slug was deliberately NOT set at creation time (only `requestedSlug`, presumably until billing completed); now the slug is claimed immediately in the billing-enabled flow and never set in the billing-disabled flow. This is unrelated to the destinationCalendar change and inverts the intended behavior of the billing gate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancelling all remaining recurring bookings only deletes the first calendar reference per booking

The recurring-cancel branch inside the new per-reference loop still does `const bookingRef = updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` and deletes only that one event, and it iterates only `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's). With multiple hosts, each updated booking now has several `_calendar` references (one per host credential), so the other hosts' recurring instances are never deleted. Additionally, because this whole block is now nested inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`, the entire delete-across-all-credentials routine runs once per reference, issuing duplicate delete calls for the same events.

Confirming a collective booking still builds evt with a single destination calendar

For bookings requiring confirmation, calendar events are created at confirmation time via `handleConfirmation`/`EventManager.create(evt)`, but the `evt` built here sets `destinationCalendar` to only `[booking.destinationCalendar]` or `[user.destinationCalendar]` — the organizer's single calendar. The per-host destination calendars of the other collective hosts are never added, so confirming a collective opt-in booking still only creates the event on the organizer's calendar — the exact bug this PR sets out to fix remains in the confirmation path. The same gap exists in the payment-success flows (`packages/features/ee/payments/api/webhook.ts` and `paypal-webhook.ts`), which also build `evt` with only the booking/organizer destination calendar before calling `eventManager.create(evt)`.

Crash when location is Google Meet and destinationCalendar is empty

In `EventManager.create()` the new code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` in `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")`. When the event has no destination calendar (e.g. organizer and event type both have none, which `handleNewBooking` now represents as `null`), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError, failing the whole booking. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and safely fell back to Cal Video in exactly this scenario — this is the very fallback the comment describes ('Google Meet selected w/o a Google Cal'). Needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId after primary fallback

In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that writes the hangout link into the description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When no destination calendar matches the credential (the "primary" fallback path), `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`, so the patch targets `calendars/undefined/...` and the event description never gets the Meet link. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always at least "primary".

Reschedule only deletes the first old calendar event, leaving stale events on other hosts' calendars

In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, when `newBookingId` is set (reschedule), the cleanup of the old booking's calendar events uses `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))` — a single reference. Now that this PR creates one `_calendar` reference per collective-event host, the old booking can have several calendar references, and only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep the stale pre-reschedule event on their calendars. This should iterate over all old calendar references (filter) and delete each with its own credentialId/externalCalendarId.

Reschedule-request deletes calendar events with the organizer's credential instead of each reference's credential

Calendar cleanup here builds `credentialsMap` from the requesting user's credentials keyed by type, then for every booking reference calls `getCalendar(credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type))` and deletes `bookingRef.uid`. With this PR, collective bookings have references pointing at OTHER hosts' credentials/calendars; deleting those events with the organizer's credential of the same app type will not find the event (different account), so the other hosts' calendar events survive a reschedule request. The per-reference `credentialId` (now stored thanks to this PR) should be used to load the correct credential, as done in `handleCancelBooking`.

destinationCalendar falls back to null here but [] everywhere else, and team calendars are silently dropped when null

The new evt initializer uses `: null` when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar, while every other call site in this PR (confirm, cancel, payment webhooks, bookingReminder, etc.) uses `[]`. This makes the webhook payload shape inconsistent (BOOKING_CREATED/BOOKING_REQUESTED send `destinationCalendar: null`, BOOKING_REJECTED sends `[]`), which consumers must special-case — the e2e expectations updated in this PR encode exactly that inconsistency. Additionally, the subsequent `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when the value is null, so for a collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar, the other hosts' calendars are silently discarded.

loadUsers refactor drops organization.slug from dynamic booking user query

The rewritten `loadUsers` for the dynamic (no eventTypeId) path selects `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` but no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` that the old query included. Any downstream code reading `user.organization?.slug` for dynamic collective bookings (org context/branding/URLs) will now get `undefined`. This change is also unrelated to the destinationCalendar fix.

updateLocation creates new references without externalCalendarId/credentialId

In `updateLocation`, `referencesToCreate` now uses `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but these results come from `updateAllCalendarEvents` → `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, whose returned `EventResult` never sets `externalId` or `credentialId`. Previously these were populated from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`/`?.credentialId`. `editLocation.handler` then persists these references (`references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`), so after a location edit the new references lack the credential/calendar ids that later update/delete flows depend on.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Placeholder refresh_token = "refresh_token" overwrites real refresh tokens in the database

When a refresh response omits `refresh_token`, the code writes the literal string "refresh_token" into the result. office365calendar then merges this over the stored credential (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and zoomvideo assigns `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` directly, and both persist it. If the sync feature is later disabled, or a provider omits refresh_token in a normal refresh, the credential's real refresh token is permanently replaced with the placeholder and all future refreshes fail with invalid_grant, requiring the user to reconnect.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema drops expiry and refresh_token — computed keys collapse and zod strips unknown fields

The schema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`; both evaluate to "[object Object]", so the second overwrites the first, and the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. Because zod strips unknown keys by default, parsing any token response returns only `{ access_token }` — the comments claiming "any property with a number is the expiry" are wrong. Consequences in the sync path: in zoomvideo `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` becomes NaN (which then fails zoomTokenSchema's z.number() on the next read, breaking Zoom entirely), and office365calendar never updates its stored expiry.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential-sync refresh path returns a raw fetch Response, but the code reads res.data and crashes

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response from the sync endpoint, which has no `.data` property and whose body is never parsed. The normal path returns GaxiosResponse (`fetchTokens.res`) which does have `.data`. So in the sync path `const token = res?.data` is `undefined` and `googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block treats it as a non-'invalid_grant' error and silently returns myGoogleAuth with the old, expired credentials, so every Google Calendar API call for synced users fails with 401s and the credential is never marked invalid.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
