true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes via NullPointerException from the unwired factory, not via the intended validation

The test builds DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory by calling init() and hand-populating grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts, but never calls postInit(), so the sessionFactory field stays null. Decoding "ofrtac:5678" enters the lazy-refresh branch of getGrantTypeByShortcut(), which dereferences sessionFactory and throws NullPointerException; the broad catch (RuntimeException) then lets the test pass. The intended IllegalArgumentException path ("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type") and the lazy map-refresh logic in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut are therefore never actually exercised, and the test would still pass if that logic were broken or removed.

The candidate issue goes a step further to explain the severe consequence of this broad catch (it masks a NullPointerException caused by incomplete initialization, making the test pass for the wrong reason), which directly validates and expands upon the golden comment's concern.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom OAuth2 grant type providers at server startup

Adding an abstract method to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface means any existing third-party/custom grant-type provider compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError as soon as getShortcut() is invoked on it. That invocation happens eagerly for every registered grant factory in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit(), i.e. during server boot, so upgrading with an existing custom grant provider deployed makes Keycloak fail to start with an obscure error. A default method (for example returning the "na"/unknown shortcut, or deriving a shortcut from the provider id) would keep existing implementations working.

Only the standard token-exchange provider records the grant type; other exchange flows mint tokens with "na" grant

Constants.GRANT_TYPE is set on the client session context only in StandardTokenExchangeProvider. The legacy (V1) token exchange provider and the other V2 exchange providers (subject impersonation, federated) create access tokens through the same TokenManager paths without ever setting this attribute, so access tokens they issue are encoded with the "na" (unknown) grant shortcut instead of "te". Since a stated motivation of this PR is to reliably know the grant type for token-exchange use cases (#37117), the signal will be missing/misleading for those exchange flows.

Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed after successful use

When a user's recovery codes live in a user-storage provider (the capability this PR adds), a successfully used code is never invalidated. For locally stored codes, single-use semantics are enforced inside RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid(), which removes the used code from the stored credential. In the federated path, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid() calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...), which delegates to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid(), and the framework performs no consumption step afterwards. The PR's own reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) only compares the presented code against the stored list and never removes it. Consequences: every recovery code remains valid indefinitely, breaking the one-time-use guarantee of the feature; RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() never becomes true, so the user is never forced to regenerate codes and the login form always asks for code #1; and even if a storage did consume codes itself, the cleanup call authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) operates on Keycloak's local credential store and cannot remove a credential living in user storage. The feature needs a consumption/update mechanism for federated credentials (e.g., writing the reduced code list back through CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential after a successful validation) or the limitation must be explicitly handled.

Plaintext recovery codes are pushed to user storage while local storage keeps only hashes

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and sends them to the user storage via a UserCredentialModel. When the same credential is stored locally, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues() hashes every code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode() so only hashes are persisted (verification is done with verifyRecoveryCodeInput against the hash). Unlike OTP secrets — which an external store genuinely needs in clear text to compute TOTP — recovery-code verification can be performed by hashing the presented code, so there is no technical need to hand the raw codes to the user storage. As implemented, any external user storage that opts into recovery codes ends up holding every user's recovery codes in clear text (and the codes transit in clear through CredentialInput.getChallengeResponse()), so a read-breach of that store, its backups, or its logs exposes all of a user's recovery codes. Consider sending hashed codes to the storage and documenting that storages should hash the presented code in isValid(), matching the local storage security posture.

New recovery-keys test never verifies single-use semantics

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin performs only one successful login with one recovery code. It never attempts to reuse the same code, never checks that the remaining-code count decreases, and never exercises the all-codes-used path (credential removal and re-adding the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action). Because of this, the test passes even though recovery codes stored in user storage are currently reusable after a successful login — the core security property of the feature is unverified. The test should at minimum assert that a second login attempt with the same code fails and that a subsequent login requests a different code number.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION overstates when the rolling-updates feature must be enabled

The new CAUTION says: "While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail." Read literally this tells every reader that any deployment without the preview feature will break, but that is only true when an explicit update strategy is configured. With the default (unset) `spec.update.strategy` the Operator mimics 26.1 behavior and never invokes the update-compatibility command, so it works fine without the feature — this PR's own UpgradeTest demonstrates it: `createInitialDeployment` returns early for the null strategy without enabling `rolling-updates`, and `testCacheMaxCount(null)` still expects a successful rolling-upgrade status. The statement should be scoped (e.g., "must be enabled when configuring `spec.update.strategy`"), otherwise users on the default strategy may wrongly conclude they must enable a preview feature to keep the Operator working.

New and changed update-compatibility exit codes are never asserted

This PR introduces a new exit code (FEATURE_DISABLED = 4, returned when `rolling-updates` is not enabled) and changes the recreate exit code from 4 to 3 in CompatibilityResult, and the update-compatibility guide explicitly tells users to build automation around these exit codes rather than log output. However, no test verifies them: `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr message (line 49) and never checks that the process exits with code 4, and `testWrongVersions`/`testCompatible` assert messages but never assert exit code 3 (recreate required) or 0 (rolling possible) for the `check` command. A future regression that swaps or drops these exit codes — the tool's documented scripting contract — would pass the test suite unnoticed. Please add exitCode assertions to these tests.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting any client throws UnsupportedOperationException when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener (AdminPermissions.java:90-91) handles every ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). With the v2 feature on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose new clients() override now returns ClientPermissionsV2, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The new guard added to the listener checks Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1), which is also enabled whenever v2 is enabled (v2 presupposes v1), so it does not protect this path. Provider events are published synchronously inside the transaction, so the exception propagates out of the client-removal call, rolls back the transaction and returns a 500 — deleting a client (and any realm teardown that removes clients) is broken under v2. Before this PR the event was dispatched to the v1 ClientPermissions implementation, which successfully removed the client's v2 authorization resources (they live on the same admin-permissions resource server, named by client id), so this is a regression introduced by the clients() override. Either implement the disable/cleanup path in ClientPermissionsV2 or skip this event for v2 in the listener. None of the added tests exercise deleting a client with v2 enabled, which is why this is not caught.

canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles drop the manage/admin-role fallback, denying legitimate admins

The v1 ClientPermissions implementations of canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles and canMapClientScopeRoles all start with `if (canManage(client)) return true;`, i.e. a caller with the manage-clients admin role (or manage permission on the client) may map roles. UserPermissionsV2.canMapRoles keeps the same fallback (this PR's own testTransitiveUserPermissions asserts that all-users MANAGE implies map-roles for users). The new ClientPermissionsV2 overrides (lines 91-103) only evaluate the FGAP MAP_ROLES / MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE / MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE permissions. Consequence: as soon as the v2 feature flag is enabled, a realm admin holding the manage-clients role but no FGAP policies gets 403 from RoleMapperResource.addClientRoleMapping, addComposites, etc. — in every realm, including realms that never opted into admin permissions, because hasPermission() returns false when the realm has no admin-permissions resource server (root.realmResourceServer() == null). Note that AdminPermissions.evaluator() selects MgmtPermissionsV2 based on the profile flag alone, not on realm opt-in. Add `if (canManage(client)) return true;` to the three methods for parity with v1 and with users v2.

getResourceName has no branch for the Clients resource type

getResourceName resolves Users resources to the user's username and labels the all-users resource "All users", but nothing handles the new Clients type. Permission representations for client resources therefore fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never populated for resources created by getOrCreateResource, so the admin API/console shows a null/empty name (or the raw internal client UUID) instead of the clientId, and the all-clients resource gets no friendly label analogous to "All users". Add a Clients branch that resolves ClientModel.getClientId() and an "All clients" label for the type resource.

Javadoc for requireView()/requireViewClientScopes() describes return values of void methods; v2 notes misdescribe the fallback

The newly added javadoc for the void methods requireView() (line 96) and requireViewClientScopes() (line 101) says "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true" — copied from the can* methods; these methods return nothing and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. In addition, the repeated "For V2 only: Also if the caller has a permission to <scope> for all clients" notes are inaccurate: the v2 implementation checks the specific client's resource first and only falls back to the all-clients resource when no client-specific resource exists, so a client-specific grant (not just an all-clients grant) also satisfies the check. The documentation should describe the actual contract for implementers of this interface.

Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

The callback passes groupResource.getId() (the Resource entity UUID) to hasPermission, which looks it up with resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) — that never matches, so evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource instead of each group's own resource, and per-group view-members/manage-members permissions are never detected. It then adds groupResource.getId() (again the wrong UUID) into the granted set; callers put this set into the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute (UsersResource.searchForUser, BruteForceUsersResource) and into getUsersCount, which filter by group ids. Consequences: (a) for per-group grants the DB-level group restriction is never applied, so user searches run unfiltered with pagination applied before the canView post-filter (wrong pages, wrong counts); (b) when an admin has view-members on ALL groups, the all-groups resource (name 'Groups', not a group id) matches the iteration and its resource UUID is added as a bogus group id, so user search returns nothing and count returns 0 for an admin who should see everyone. getOrCreateResource creates the per-group resource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId()) and updates its scopes, but never calls setType (compare V1 GroupPermissions.initialize, which explicitly calls groupResource.setType("Group")). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission enumerates group resources with resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...); since resources created here have a null type, they are never enumerated — only the 'Groups' all-resource (whose type is set in init()) matches. The same gap exists for per-user/per-client resources created through this method, but it only becomes observable with the new Groups findByType usage.

getResourceName is the mechanism that translates per-object authorization resources into human-readable names for display (for Users it returns "All users" for the type resource and the username otherwise). The advertised feature provides no working functionality; it should either be implemented against a real mechanism or removed, with negative offsets rejected up front.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No guard against concurrent BuildIndex for the same key after removing the whole-function lock

BuildIndex now only locks cacheMu for the final cache insert, and nothing prevents two goroutines from building the same NamespacedResource concurrently: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex checks GetIndex and then builds outside any lock (its own TODO acknowledges this), so two simultaneous Search requests, or a watch event racing a search, for a namespace that was skipped at startup (below InitMinCount) or newly created will both call BuildIndex. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both call bleve.New on the same directory, so one fails with a store-lock/already-exists error that is surfaced to the user even though nothing is actually wrong; for in-memory indexes one fully built index is silently discarded by the last cache write and IndexTenants is double-counted. The previous whole-function mutex at least serialized these duplicate builds. A per-key lock or singleflight around check-build-cache would fix it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same concurrency/race condition bug described in the golden comment: moving `cacheMu` from protecting the whole `BuildIndex` function to only protecting the final cache insert allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same index for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and counter in concurrent index build loop

In searchSupport.init, every goroutine spawned via group.Go writes to the outer err variable (`_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)`) and increments totalBatchesIndexed without any synchronization. With initWorkers > 1 (the whole point of this PR is concurrent namespace builds), these are concurrent reads/writes of shared variables: a Go data race that will fail under -race, the trace event count (span.AddEvent using totalBatchesIndexed) can be wrong, and worse, the closure returns the shared err — if goroutine A's build fails but goroutine B overwrites err with nil before A's `return err` is evaluated, errgroup sees nil and startup succeeds with a failed/missing index. Use a local variable inside the closure (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and an atomic counter (or compute the count from len(stats)).

Watch goroutine panics on closed events channel and uses a never-canceled context

The watch loop started at the end of searchSupport.init uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (so it is never canceled on server shutdown) and then does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` without checking the receive's ok flag. The SQL backend's poller closes the events channel when the backend stops; receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately, so handleEvent dereferences a nil *WrittenEvent at `evt.Type` — an unrecovered panic in this goroutine crashes the entire process during shutdown (and absent the panic the loop would spin at 100% CPU). Because this PR makes init run unconditionally at server construction, this goroutine now always starts. It should be `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`, and the context should be tied to the server lifecycle. Note the same unguarded-receive pattern exists in initWatcher in server.go.

No test coverage for the new eager-init contract

NewResourceServer now runs s.Init synchronously and returns an error when backend init or the index build fails, and the s.Init(ctx) guards were removed from every gRPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) — but no test was added or updated to cover the new contract: that construction-time init failures propagate, or that handlers behave correctly without ever calling Init. false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() destroys the factory-owned shared queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (also reached via terminate() and join()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory: it is created once in the factory's __init__ and the same instance is passed to every strategy produced by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()+join() on the strategy at every partition revocation/rebalance and then builds a new strategy from the same factory. After the first rebalance the pool's queues have been shut down (queue.Queue.shutdown()) and all worker threads have exited, so every subsequent queue_pool.submit() raises queue.ShutDown from work_queue.put(); that exception is swallowed by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's except clause, which marks the offset complete so it is committed even though the message was never processed. Net effect: after any routine consumer-group event (deploy, scaling, assignment change) a consumer in thread-queue-parallel mode silently drops all results until the process is restarted. The pool lifecycle should belong only to the factory (strategy.close() should stop just its own commit thread), or the factory should create a fresh pool in create_with_partitions().

submit()'s catch-all marks offsets complete for messages that were never processed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the broad `except Exception` handler records the message's offset via add_offset + complete_offset, making it committable even though the message was never handed to a worker. Skipping is intentional for undecodable payloads, but those are already handled by decode_payload returning None; this catch-all also fires for real failures — grouping_fn raising, or work_queue.put raising queue.ShutDown once the pool has been shut down (after a rebalance, or during shutdown with in-flight submits). In those cases the offset is committed and the result is silently lost instead of being left uncommitted so it can be re-consumed. Only the intentional skip path (decoder returned None) should complete the offset; unexpected exceptions from grouping/submission should propagate or leave the offset outstanding so the message is retried.

Queues are unbounded, so the advertised 'natural backpressure' does not exist

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so they are unbounded. The class and strategy docstrings advertise 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but an unbounded queue never fills: if workers fall behind on slow results (the exact problem this PR is meant to mitigate), submit() never blocks and the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffering WorkItem objects — each retaining the full original Kafka message — in memory without limit. Under sustained lag this grows memory unboundedly and can OOM the consumer, and it defeats the offset-based flow control since offsets are only committed after processing. Give the queues a maxsize (or otherwise cap in-flight items) so put() blocks and provides real backpressure.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker shutdown flags before draining, so queued items are abandoned

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() first sets worker.shutdown = True for every worker and only then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on `while not self.shutdown`, so a worker that finishes its current item after the flag is set exits its loop immediately, abandoning any items still in its queue — the immediate=False 'drain remaining items' semantics never take effect because no worker is left to read them. Those messages were already fetched from Kafka; their offsets simply never get committed and they will be reprocessed on restart, but the shutdown is not actually graceful as written. Shut the queues down first (immediate=False) so workers drain and then exit via queue.ShutDown, and only use the flag as a backstop.

test_stats_reporting races with workers draining the queue

In test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 items to a pool whose workers process each item in microseconds, then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0. Whether anything is still queued at that point is a race between the submitting thread and the three worker threads; on a fast machine the workers can drain all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making this assertion fail intermittently. The test should hold items in the queue with an explicit blocking condition in the processor before asserting non-zero depth, or drop that assertion.

false_positives.candidate:
Set→sorted-set change will WRONGTYPE-fail on segment keys written before the deploy

Segment keys (`span-buf:s:*`) were previously plain Redis sets written with SADD; this PR switches all access to sorted-set commands (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). Existing keys live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), so after a rolling deploy, any batch or flush touching a pre-deploy key raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` — the Lua EVALSHA aborts and `p.execute()` raises, failing the whole Kafka batch until those keys expire or are flushed. There is no migration step or type-tolerant handling; this needs an explicit rollout plan (flush the buffer cluster, or drain before enabling).

max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; the only enforcement is a hardcoded 1000 in Lua

The Python-side guard in `_load_segment_data` that skipped segments exceeding `self.max_segment_spans` (and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) was deleted, but `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001). The only remaining enforcement is the hardcoded `if span_count > 1000` in add-buffer.lua, which neither matches the default (1001) nor any configured value — anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` now gets a silent no-op, and the span-count cap diverges from the documented setting. Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or remove the parameter.

ZUNIONSTORE default AGGREGATE SUM doubles scores of duplicated spans, skewing eviction

`zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` uses Redis's default AGGREGATE SUM, so when the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a duplicate/redelivered span that was previously merged), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps — roughly 2× the real time. Since eviction is `zpopmin` (lowest score first), such a duplicated span is artificially protected from eviction and will survive while genuinely newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so duplicated members keep a sane score.

Redirect-chain limit lowered from 10000 to 1000; over-limit chains silently mis-join segments

The redirect resolution loop now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000. When the limit is hit the loop simply ends with `set_span_id` pointing at a mid-chain span, and the incoming span is merged into that mid-chain set (recreating an unlinked key as a new orphan segment) rather than the segment root — fragmenting the segment into separately flushed pieces. Redirect entries persist for `redis_ttl` (1h) for every span id ever seen, independent of the new 1000-span payload cap, so very active traces can still build chains longer than 1000. If the lower bound is intentional, at least log or metric when the loop exits without resolving (redirect_depth == 1000) so the fragmentation is observable.

end_timestamp_precise is used as a Redis score without validation; one bad span fails the whole batch

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is passed straight through as the ZADD score for the span payload. `rapidjson.loads` accepts NaN/Infinity, and Redis rejects non-finite ZADD scores with an error, so a single malformed span makes the entire `p.execute()` pipeline fail — failing and reprocessing the whole Kafka batch rather than just the bad span. Previously the payload went into a plain set so this value was never interpreted. Sanitize the score (e.g. skip or clamp non-finite values) before building the ZADD mapping.

Accidental nested git submodule (gitlink) committed

This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d2909...`, i.e. a gitlink pinning a nested checkout of the sentry repository itself (at this PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is almost certainly an accidental artifact of having a local clone inside the working tree. Once merged, every checkout of the repo will contain an uninitializable submodule directory, `git status` will permanently show it, and CI/checkout tooling that recurses or validates submodules may fail. It should be removed from the PR.

upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no NULL fallback, silently dropping unsampled errors

The new `upsampled_count()` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum()` skips NULL values, so any error event whose `sample_weight` is NULL contributes 0 to the count. NULL weights occur for events ingested before the project was allowlisted / before the column existed, and for events the SDK/Relay sent without an `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` context (e.g. projects at sample rate 1.0 that never attach the context). The code comments assert 'sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects', but nothing enforces this: the allowlist is a mutable option applied to projects with pre-existing data. Consequence: for allowlisted projects, `count()` becomes an undercount that silently excludes exactly those events, which is worse than not upsampling at all. The aggregate should coalesce missing weights, e.g. `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, toFloat64(1)))` (or `ifNull(sample_weight, 1)`), so unsampled events count once. Note the new snuba tests only store events that carry the `error_sampling` context, so this failure mode is not covered anywhere.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring matching on the raw query string, producing false positives

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET['query']` and checks `'event.type:error' in query`. This is not a parsed search match: a query like `message:"saw event.type:error in logs"` or a longer value such as `event.type:errortag` contains the substring and will be classified as error-focused. The `count()` → `sum(sample_weight)` transform is then applied to a query that also matches transactions/other events, whose `sample_weight` is NULL, so those events are counted as 0 and the returned counts are wrong. If the intent is to only transform queries that filter to error events, the query should be parsed (or at minimum token-boundary matched) rather than substring-matched.

upsampled_count registered without private=True, exposing an internal-only function in the public query API

The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` does not set `private=True`, unlike the sibling internal helper directly above it in `function_converter`. Public functions are selectable by any API user in arbitrary discover/events queries (`upsampled_count()` in `field`/`yAxis`) and may surface in docs/function-listing surfaces. Since this function is an implementation detail of the error-upsampling feature (injected by the endpoint itself, which works regardless of visibility) and returns misleading values on non-allowlisted or unsampled data, it should be marked `private=True` to keep it out of the public query surface.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. true_positives.matched_candidate:

The key is built as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent with no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so two different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key: e.g. (name="dash_1", parent="x") and (name="dash", parent="1_x") both yield "..._dash_1_x". A denial cached for one resource would then incorrectly deny a different resource/parent combination for up to the 30s TTL. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys using simple string concatenation with underscores, which allows key collisions if the components themselves contain underscores, leading to incorrect permission denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is consulted before the permission cache, so a stale denial overrides fresher cached grants

In Check, the denial cache is checked first (lines 116-121) and returns Allowed=false immediately, before the cached permission set is consulted (line 123). Denial entries live for shortCacheTTL (30s) and are never invalidated. Consider: (1) a user is denied resource A after a DB requery, so a denial entry for A is cached; (2) the user is then granted A in the DB; (3) any other cache miss for the same user+action re-queries the DB and refreshes permCache, which now includes A; (4) a new Check for A hits the stale denial entry and returns false even though the server's own fresh permCache would allow it. This reintroduces the exact 'user can't access a resource they were just granted' problem this PR is meant to fix, for up to 30s after any denial. Checking the cached permissions first (allow on positive evidence, then consult the denial cache for the fast-deny path) would avoid contradicting fresher cached grants while keeping the denial fast path.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

GitHub usernames are mutable and recyclable: (a) if the user who installed the app later renames their GitHub account, the stored sender login no longer matches and that legitimate user can never link or re-link the installation; (b) conversely, if an attacker registers the abandoned old username, they satisfy this check and can attach the victim's GitHub App installation (installation IDs are sequential and guessable) to their own Sentry organization. In update(), the "original" IdP passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is obtained via getById(...), which wraps the model with createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel when the organization feature is enabled. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to additionally require the linked organization to be enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then evaluates LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() (which includes isEnabled()) on this wrapped original but on the raw updated model, so the two sides are not comparable — and neither matches what defines cache membership, since the cached login lists are filled by idpDelegate.getForLogin(...), which filters on the raw persisted enabled flag. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, releases it, and then acquires the write lock at line 48 — but never re-checks the cache once the write lock is held. When multiple requests race before the cache is first populated (e.g. at startup), each one sequentially re-opens and re-parses assets-manifest.json and overwrites the cache, defeating most of the benefit of the fix. Worse, if goroutine B populates the cache successfully and goroutine A's redundant re-read then fails (file removed during startup, transient I/O error), line 69 stores nil over the valid cache and A returns an error to its caller even though assets were already loaded. Add a second nil check after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking) so only the first caller performs the load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `GetWebAssets` implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern by failing to re-check if the cache was populated after upgrading from a read lock to a write lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, releases it, and then acquires the write lock at line 48 — but never re-checks the cache once the write lock is held. When multiple requests race before the cache is first populated (e.g. at startup), each one sequentially re-opens and re-parses assets-manifest.json and overwrites the cache, defeating most of the benefit of the fix. Worse, if goroutine B populates the cache successfully and goroutine A's redundant re-read then fails (file removed during startup, transient I/O error), line 69 stores nil over the valid cache and A returns an error to its caller even though assets were already loaded. Add a second nil check after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking) so only the first caller performs the load.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment specifically addresses the unconditional assignment to the cache even when an error occurs (alongside acknowledging the missing double-check). The candidate issue identifies both the missing double-checked locking and the exact consequence mentioned in the golden comment: 'if goroutine B populates the cache successfully and goroutine A's redundant re-read then fails..., line 69 stores nil over the valid cache'. Since the candidate explicitly points out the bug at line 69 where a failed fetch overwrites a valid cache with nil, it captures the core issue described in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across file (and potential network) I/O

The write lock is taken at line 48 and held via defer for the entire remainder of GetWebAssets, which includes the assets-manifest.json read at line 60 and — if the cdn variable at line 54 is ever set to a non-empty value as the comment suggests — a CDN HTTP fetch via http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout. While one caller performs that I/O, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks on the mutex, including callers that would have been satisfied by the already-populated cache; in dev mode (where the cache is never consulted) this serializes every call. Consider performing the load outside the critical section and taking the write lock only to publish the result, combined with the double-check described above.

No regression test for the data race being fixed

This PR exists to fix a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache, but it adds no test that would catch a regression. A test that invokes GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines (with cfg.Env != setting.Dev so the cache path is exercised) and is run under `go test -race` would fail before this change and pass after it. Without such a test, a future refactor of this function can silently reintroduce the unsynchronized access, and CI will not notice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs

The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. It makes every cleanup job run 10x more often — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, and query history (the last of which runs several DELETE/count queries each cycle) — multiplying background database and filesystem load for all Grafana instances. Inline ID list for SQLite built with O(n^2) string concatenation

Each iteration reallocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of N IDs costs O(N^2) in bytes copied — with the batch size of 32767 exercised by the new test that is on the order of several GB of copying per batch, and the tag cleanup runs the same path with even more IDs. This runs on every cleanup cycle when a large batch size is configured. Using a strings.Builder (or strings.Join on a pre-converted []string) with strconv.AppendInt would make it linear.

In TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, each subtest creates its annotations and runs assertions (which use require, aborting the subtest on failure) before registering t.Cleanup at line 120. Because createTestAnnotations now inserts rows with explicit primary keys (ID: int64(i+1), line 241) and all subtests share the same fakeSQL database, any failure before the cleanup is registered leaves rows behind, and every subsequent subtest then fails with primary-key conflicts on IDs 1..N rather than its actual assertion result, making the real failure hard to diagnose. Registering the t.Cleanup before createTestAnnotations (so tables are truncated even on early failure) avoids the cascade.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with the object name as the resource label

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name in the position where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind`. If the third argument is the metric's resource label (as all the kind-based call sites indicate), this creates a Prometheus series per deleted object name — unbounded cardinality that grows with every object — and breaks per-kind aggregation/alerting for the delete method. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: passing `name` instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods in the file.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and are cancelled when the request completes

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming apiserver request context. For server requests, the context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which happens immediately after the dual writer returns its response. The 10-second timeout therefore almost never gets to run: every legacy write races with request teardown and will frequently fail with context.Canceled. Since the failure is only recorded in a metric and never logged, mode 3 silently drops the 'safety' legacy writes it exists to perform, leaving legacy and unified storage permanently diverged with no signal. The goroutine context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (which preserves values like the logger and user) before applying the timeout.

Legacy goroutine reuses the request object that unified storage may have mutated and that is being serialized for the response

The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` with the same `runtime.Object` pointer that was just handed to `d.Storage.Create`. k8s-style stores mutate the object passed to Create/Update (setting UID, resourceVersion, generation, timestamps) and typically return that same pointer as `created`. If unified storage does that, the legacy goroutine and the HTTP handler then concurrently mutate and serialize the same object: the legacy store can overwrite unified's resourceVersion/UID on the object being written to the response — a data race and a potentially corrupted response body. Previously the legacy call was synchronous so mutation ordering was controlled; making it async requires passing `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the legacy call (same concern applies to the Update path reusing request-scoped objects).

Unordered async legacy writes can leave legacy permanently stale (lost updates)

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering guarantees. Two quick successive updates to the same object (or a create immediately followed by an update) can be applied to legacy out of order: the goroutine carrying the newer update may finish before the older one, which then overwrites legacy with stale data. Because legacy errors are only counted in a metric and never logged, nothing surfaces this divergence, and the legacy copy — the stated purpose of mode 3 ('just as a safe measure') — can silently remain at an old revision indefinitely. Legacy writes need per-object serialization (e.g. a single ordered worker/queue) and/or resourceVersion-based conflict handling.

Async legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere

In all four write methods the error from the async legacy call is only passed to `recordLegacyDuration`; the previous implementation logged it (e.g. `log.Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`). For a mode whose purpose is keeping legacy as a safety net, a failing safety net with no log entry makes diagnosis impossible — this would also have made the request-context cancellation bug visible in logs. Log the error with object identifiers inside each goroutine.

Mode 3 unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens

The legacy expectations are registered on a testify mock that is shared between the legacy and unified mocks (both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`), and the tests return immediately after the dual-writer call without waiting for the legacy goroutine or calling AssertExpectations. Consequences: (a) the success cases pass even if the legacy call never runs — the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go fails nothing here; (b) because both backends share one mock, the Create error case registers only a 'legacy' expectation and it is actually `Storage.Create` that matches it, so the test's name and setup do not reflect what is exercised. Use separate mocks and wait/assert on the legacy invocation (e.g. require.Eventually) so each backend's call and ordering is genuinely checked.

New mode-3 playlist subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous legacy writes and will be flaky

`doPlaylistTests` performs k8s writes and then immediately reads through the legacy API (`getFromBothAPIs`, the 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' subtest, and the `/api/playlists` list comparisons) expecting both backends to agree. Under mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these cross-backend assertions race the legacy goroutine — they pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling (and fail outright whenever the legacy write is cancelled at request end, per the context bug in dualwriter_mode3.go). The two new mode-3 runs of this shared test need to poll for convergence on the legacy side (e.g. require.Eventually) or use relaxed expectations.

The authn service/middleware maps typed authn errors to specific status codes, but an untyped error like this is treated as an internal failure: the anonymous user gets an HTTP 500 (and an error log entry) rather than a deliberate response such as 401/429 with a meaningful message. The relative-URL rewrite treats any href/src starting with '/' as host-relative: a protocol-relative URL like //cdn.example.com/a.png matches `href.start_with?('/')` and is rewritten to http://blog.example.com/cdn.example.com/a.png, producing a broken link. Protocol-relative URLs are common in feed/article HTML. The check should exclude values starting with '//' (and ideally also absolutize paths that don't start with '/', which are currently left relative and break in the forum context).

URIs that pass the regex but are invalid crash the whole import run

URLs are only validated against /^https?:\/\// before URI(url) is called in absolutize_urls (and open(url) in import_remote). Feed links or embed URLs containing spaces or other characters illegal in URIs (e.g. 'http://example.com/my post.html') pass the regex but raise URI::InvalidURIError here, which is not rescued — in PollFeed this aborts the entire hourly run so no further feed items are imported, and in the RetrieveTopic job it causes repeated sidekiq retries. Validate with URI.parse in a begin/rescue and skip bad items instead of aborting.

ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT + NOT NULL rewrites the entire posts table and blocks writes

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false forces PostgreSQL (< 11) to rewrite every row of the posts table while holding an AccessExclusiveLock. posts is the largest table in a Discourse install, so on any sizable forum this migration blocks all posting/reading for minutes during a deploy. Safer pattern: add the column without a default, backfill in batches, then set the default and the NOT NULL constraint.

Find-then-create race on embed_url unique index aborts concurrent import jobs

import does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and later TopicEmbed.create! inside a transaction. Two concurrent jobs for the same URL (a RetrieveTopic job racing the hourly PollFeed, or two RetrieveTopic jobs for staff, who bypass the redis throttle) both see no existing embed and both build a topic and post; the second create! hits the unique index on topic_embeds.embed_url and raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, failing that job — and in PollFeed, aborting the rest of the feed items. Rescue RecordNotUnique/re-check inside the transaction or use an upsert-style create_or_find.

Non-atomic setnx + expire can permanently throttle an embed URL

retrieved_recently? does $redis.setnx(retrieved_key, '1') followed by a separate $redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60). If the process crashes (or expire raises) between the two calls, the key never expires and retrieve() will treat that embed_url as recently retrieved forever — the topic is never fetched. Use a single atomic SET with an EX option (supported by redis-rb) instead of the two-step dance.

Editing an already-released migration and adding force: true

This changes the shipped 20131223171005_create_top_topics migration to create_table :top_topics, force: true. Databases that already ran the migration will never re-run it, so the change is a silent no-op there; on fresh or restored setups, force: true will silently DROP and recreate the table (and any data) if it already exists. Released migrations shouldn't be modified — add a new migration instead. The new db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb uses force: true too, carrying the same silent-drop risk.

The tests 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' never enable the preceding conditions: feed_polling_enabled? defaults to false in the test env (and the URL is unset in the username test), so execute short-circuits at the first condition and `poller.expects(:poll_feed).never` passes regardless of the condition under test. These specs would still pass if the url/username presence checks were removed entirely. Each gating test should stub all the prior conditions to true so only the condition under test fails.

false_positives.candidate:
Busy times are ignored on date-override days, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the code reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (lines 133-135) and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function is ever evaluated. `busy` contains the host's existing Cal.com bookings and external calendar events, so on any day that has a date override, none of the host's actual commitments block slots. This applies to fixed hosts in round-robin/collective events, to loose hosts (the loose-host loop calls the same function), and to personal events (whose single user counts as fixed). A host who already has a booking or calendar event inside an override window can be double-booked. The early return should only skip the working-hours check; the busy check must still run.

Working-hours check rejects every slot for hosts with multiple windows per day

The new working-hours guard uses `workingHours.find(...)` and returns `false` (slot unavailable) whenever the predicate matches ANY window in which the slot does not fit. Hosts commonly define split availability on a day, e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, which produces two WorkingHours entries with the same days. Any slot is necessarily outside at least one of those windows, so `find` always returns truthy and every slot is rejected. Because checkIfIsAvailable now runs for every fixed host (including the single user of a personal event, and both hosts of collective events), any event whose host has more than one availability window per day becomes completely unbookable on all days. The logic needs to be inverted: reject only when NO window for that day fully contains the slot (e.g. `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`).

Multiple date-override windows on the same date break the availability check

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` predicate returns true (causing the slot to be rejected with `return false`) for the first override on the matching date in which the slot is NOT contained, and find() stops iterating there. With two override windows on the same date (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot at 14:30 is rejected because it is outside the first window, and a slot at 10:30 is rejected because it is outside the second window. Only a single override window per date works correctly. The check needs 'there exists an override on this date that contains the slot' semantics rather than short-circuiting on the first non-containing override.

Override containment check treats partial overlap as available and misses the exact end boundary

The conditions used to decide that a slot is outside an override are `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` and `slotStartTime > overrideEnd` (strict isAfter). Anything else — including a slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside and ends after it — is treated as 'within the override' and the host is considered available, even though part of the slot falls outside the override window. Additionally, a slot starting exactly at the override end fails the strict `isAfter` and is also treated as inside the override. For round-robin events where slots are generated from other hosts' working hours, this lets fixed hosts be booked outside their override window. Availability should require full containment: slotStart >= overrideStart && slotEnd <= overrideEnd.

Timezone-shifted date overrides that cross midnight are silently dropped

The override start/end are shifted by (inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset) and then reduced to hour/minute-of-day via `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the shift pushes the interval across midnight — e.g. a 09:00-17:00 IST override viewed from PST (offset -810 minutes shifts start to 19:30 of the previous day and end to 03:30) — the wrapped startTime (1170) becomes greater than endTime (210) whenever only one side of the interval wraps, and buildSlots silently skips the range (`if (start >= end) continue`). Meanwhile the user's regular working hours for that day were already spliced out of computedLocalAvailability, so the invitee sees the host as fully unavailable that day. Regular working hours handle midnight spanning by splitting the range; overrides need the same treatment.

Override date matching is formatted in the server's local timezone but compared to a UTC date

`dayjs(date.start)` creates a dayjs in the server machine's local timezone, and `.add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` is compared against `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`, where slotStartTime is in UTC mode. On any host not running in UTC (self-hosted instances with a TZ set, dev machines), the two sides of the comparison are rendered in different zones, so an override can be matched against the wrong day near midnight. `dayjs.utc(date.start)` should be used so both sides are in UTC.

Override timezone conversion silently depends on the server timezone when timeZone is absent

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is used to compute the organizer offset, but `timeZone` was added as an optional property on TimeRange, and dayjs.tz with an undefined zone falls back to the machine's local timezone. Any caller of getSlots that passes dateOverrides without a timeZone now gets results that depend on the server's timezone (and differ between UTC production servers and non-UTC dev machines), whereas the previous code did not consult a timezone at all. A deterministic fallback (e.g. `override.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone`) should be used.

No tests for the round-robin fixed-host scenario or for busy blocking on override days

The PR adds only one test: a personal event viewed from a different timezone. The headline fix — date overrides of a fixed host constraining a round-robin event's slots — has no test. There is also no test that an existing booking or calendar busy time still blocks a slot on a date-override day (which would have caught the regression where the busy check is skipped when a date override matches), and no coverage for hosts with multiple working-hour windows in one day or multiple override windows on one date, both of which the new checkIfIsAvailable logic handles incorrectly.

The new OR branch `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` deletes WorkflowReminder rows of any method, while the sibling branch — and this entire cron job — is explicitly SMS-only (`method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`). Today only this file writes retryCount, so the practical effect is identical, but the moment the email/WhatsApp reminder paths (which share the WorkflowReminder table, e.g. scheduleEmailReminders) start using retryCount, their reminders would be silently deleted by the SMS cron. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to the retryCount branch to keep the cleanup scoped to what this job owns.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: the `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` condition inside the `OR` clause of the deletion logic lacks the `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, causing it to potentially delete non-SMS reminders (like Email or WhatsApp).

false_positives.candidate:
retryCount update inside the catch block can throw and abort the whole cron run

The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ ... retryCount ... })` with no error handling of its own. If that update fails — for example the row was concurrently deleted by an overlapping cron run's `deleteMany` (Prisma P2025), or a transient DB error — the exception escapes the handler: every remaining reminder in `unscheduledReminders` is skipped and the cron invocation fails. Before this PR the catch block only logged, so a single failing reminder could never abort the rest of the batch. Worse, if the `update` inside the try (success or else branch) throws, the catch immediately attempts the same kind of update against the same row, so a likely failure is retried once and then propagates. The retryCount update in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch so the loop always continues.

Reminders skipped before the Twilio call never accumulate retryCount and keep getting rescheduled indefinitely

The retry counting only happens when `twilio.scheduleSMS` is actually invoked and returns falsy, or when an exception is thrown. If the reminder never reaches that call — e.g. `sendTo` is null because the booking has no `smsReminderNumber` (common for SMS_ATTENDEE workflows where the attendee gave no phone number), or `message` is empty — the `if (message?.length && ... && sendTo)` block is skipped entirely, so retryCount stays 0. Such reminders are never deleted by the new `retryCount > 1` cleanup and are re-fetched and re-processed on every cron run until their scheduledDate passes, which is exactly the endless-rescheduling problem this PR is meant to fix. Consider incrementing retryCount (or deleting the reminder outright when there is no recipient) in the path where sending is skipped.

deleteMany now filters on unindexed retryCount on every cron run

WorkflowReminder's indexes cover `[method, scheduled, scheduledDate]` and `[cancelled, scheduledDate]`, but nothing covers `retryCount`. This `deleteMany` executes on every cron invocation, and the new `OR: [ ..., { retryCount: { gt: 1 } } ]` branch cannot use the existing indexes, so on a large WorkflowReminder table each run degrades into a scan. Consider adding an index that includes retryCount (or otherwise restructuring the cleanup) along with the migration.

Comment above deleteMany no longer describes the query

The comment still says "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes reminders whose retryCount has exceeded the retry limit regardless of their scheduledDate. The comment should be updated so future readers understand that reminders are removed after two failed scheduling attempts, not only when past due.

getBaseConditions returns unparenthesized top-level OR fragments that break when composed with additional AND predicates

For org and team scopes, buildAuthorizationConditions returns a top-level OR expression (buildOrgAuthorizationCondition, lines 171-174, produces `(A) OR (B)`; buildTeamAuthorizationCondition, lines 204-207, likewise), and when there are no filters getBaseConditions returns that fragment verbatim via `return authConditions;` at line 75. The same problem exists for a lone eventTypeId filter, which is returned as `("eventTypeId" = $1) OR ("eventParentId" = $1)` without wrapping parentheses (lines 106, 119-122). The purpose of getBaseConditions() is to be embedded as the WHERE clause of larger raw queries; as soon as a caller appends `AND <predicate>` (e.g. a date-range or status filter, which insights queries typically add), SQL precedence turns `A OR B AND C` into `A OR (B AND C)`, so rows matching A are returned regardless of the appended predicate — silently wrong result sets and potentially data outside the intended filter. The OR-reduced fragments should be wrapped in parentheses before being returned.

Public findMany() removed with no replacement query path or caller migration

The PR deletes the service's only query-execution method, `findMany(findManyArgs)` (which merged caller-supplied where/select args with the authorization and filter conditions), and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()` returning a raw SQL fragment. No other files in the repo are changed, so any existing caller of `InsightsBookingService.findMany` — the old integration test was one — will fail to compile or lose functionality. If the service is already consumed elsewhere (e.g. insights tRPC handlers), those callers must be migrated to hand-written `$queryRaw` in the same PR; if it is not consumed yet, that should be stated. Verify all callers before merging.

Caching tests deleted while the caching logic remains in the service

The 'Caching' describe block, which asserted that repeated calls to getAuthorizationConditions() and getFilterConditions() return the cached conditions, was removed in this PR, but the service still implements caching via cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions (insightsBooking.ts lines 49-50 and 84-95). The caching path is now untested: a regression that drops the cache would go unnoticed and would silently re-run the membership/team database lookups on every call to these methods.

PR description misdescribes the change as a tests-only update

The description states the PR only updates the integration tests 'to work with the new Prisma.sql format that was previously converted in the service implementation', but the diff actually performs the service conversion itself (object notation → Prisma.sql) and removes the public findMany method. A reviewer following the description could skip reviewing the new authorization SQL in the service, even though the same description flags that area as HIGH RISK. The description should be corrected to cover the service changes.

This is a `Cannot find name 'prisma'` type-check failure / ReferenceError at runtime, so the build breaks and the Salesforce integration cannot work at all.

Sync-path Response object is persisted as the HubSpot credential key, destroying the stored credential

`refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when credential sync is enabled, but the result is typed/used as `HubspotToken`. In the sync path: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined so `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` sets undefined, and `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes a Response object — i.e. the stored credential key is overwritten with `{"expiryDate": null}`. The user's HubSpot credential (including the refresh token) is permanently wiped and they must reconnect the app.

Zoom refresh passes app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the self-hoster's sync endpoint, but Zoom's app slug everywhere else is "zoom" (see zoomvideo/api/callback.ts which stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new webhook endpoint which looks up `prisma.app` by slug). The platform cannot resolve "zoomvideo" to the Zoom app, so token refresh via the sync endpoint will fail for Zoom. Every other app passes its real slug ("google-calendar", "msteams", "webex", etc.).

axios response shape assumed, but sync path returns a fetch Response

The normal refresh function returns an AxiosResponse (read via `tokenInfo.data`), but `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when sync is enabled, which has no `.data`. `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, so Zoho Bigin token refresh always crashes when credential sync is enabled. The same class of mismatch applies to zohocrm.

axios/fetch response mismatch breaks ZohoCRM refresh when sync is enabled

The wrapped refresh function returns an AxiosResponse, but the sync branch of `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` with no `.data` property. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` therefore throws a TypeError; it is swallowed by `catch (e) { this.log.error(e); }`, leaving `this.accessToken` unset/stale. All subsequent Zoho CRM API calls go out with an empty or expired `Zoho-oauthtoken` header and fail, silently breaking the integration for synced users.

Webex refresh always rejects when credential sync is enabled

Unlike the other apps, webex kept validating with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`, and literal `scope`/`token_type` values. The documented sync-endpoint contract ("response should only contain the access token and expiry date") can never satisfy this schema, so `parsedToken.success` is always false and refresh always rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — Webex is broken whenever credential sync is on.

Lark refresh expects Lark's {code, data} envelope but sync endpoint returns a flat minimal payload

The sync-path response from `refreshOAuthTokens` is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>` and then read as `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, etc. The sync endpoint returns a flat `{access_token, expiry}` payload (per the documented contract in refreshOAuthTokens), so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws (or stores undefined token fields into the credential key). Lark calendar refresh is broken when credential sync is enabled.

findFirst by userId+appId can overwrite the wrong credential for multi-account apps

Cal.com allows a user to connect multiple accounts for the same app (e.g. several Google or Office 365 calendars), producing multiple Credential rows with the same userId and appId. The webhook's `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key with the pushed credentials, so the platform can silently clobber the tokens of a different account than intended. The payload needs an account identifier (e.g. email/external id) to target the correct credential.

Outbound request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication

The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no shared secret, signature, or header (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is only checked on the inbound webhook). The platform endpoint therefore cannot verify the request genuinely comes from its Cal.com instance; anyone who can reach that endpoint can request freshly refreshed third-party OAuth tokens for any user id / app. The implementation should include the shared secret (or an HMAC) so the platform can authenticate the caller.

No tests for the webhook endpoint or the sync refresh paths

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This change adds a new authenticated credential-writing endpoint and rewires token refresh for nine integrations with two divergent code paths (direct provider refresh vs. platform sync endpoint); the response-shape mismatches introduced here (axios vs fetch, GaxiosResponse vs fetch Response) are exactly the kind of regression a small unit/integration test per service would have caught.

false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the entire cancellation batch for the cron run

The new cancellation block wraps the whole for-loop in a single try/catch. If client.request throws for any one reminder (transient SendGrid error, invalid/already-cancelled batch_id, or SendGrid rejecting a cancel that is too close to the scheduled send time), execution jumps straight to the catch: (a) every remaining reminder in remindersToCancel is skipped for that run, and (b) none of the prisma.workflowReminder.delete calls collected so far actually execute, because they are only awaited after the loop via Promise.all and Prisma promises are lazy (they don't run until awaited). On the next cron run the same rows are re-fetched (still cancelled=true) and the loop aborts again at the same poisoned row, so a single bad reminder can block cancellation of all pending cancelled reminders until its own scheduledDate passes — at which point the first deleteMany in this handler silently drops the row and the email has already been sent. Each loop iteration needs its own try/catch (and each row should be deleted right after its own successful cancel) so one failure doesn't stall the queue.

Deferred-only cancellation still misses reminders cancelled close to their send time

With this PR, cancellation of scheduled emails happens exclusively in this cron job, which runs every 15 minutes and only cancels reminders whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. If a booking is cancelled shortly before a reminder's send time, the next cron run may not happen before SendGrid sends the email, and SendGrid does not allow changing the status of a scheduled send that is about to go out — so the reminder is delivered for a cancelled booking even though the cancellation was recorded in time. Consider using the immediate path (deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true, already used in the reschedule flow) for reminders whose scheduledDate is near (e.g. within the next hour), and deferring only far-future cancellations to the cron. That still avoids the 100-pending-cancellations limit while closing the last-minute gap.

Newly added reschedule reminder-cancellation is fire-and-forget

In the reschedule flow, the loop that cancels the original booking's workflow reminders calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...) without awaiting them, and the surrounding try/catch cannot observe their completion (the functions also swallow their own errors). If the serverless invocation is frozen after the response is sent before these promises finish, the original booking's SendGrid batches are never cancelled while the new booking's reminders are scheduled — so both old and new reminders fire, the duplicate-reminder bug for rescheduled bookings this PR is meant to fix. The cancelled flag / row deletion these calls perform is the only thing preventing reminders for the cancelled booking from being sent, so for reliability they should be collected and awaited rather than left floating in a serverless handler.

In deleteScheduledSMSReminder, if twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId) throws (transient error, or the message was already sent), the catch skips the prisma.workflowReminder.delete call. The row is then left behind with scheduled=true and cancelled unset, and — unlike the email path, which flags rows for the cron to retry — nothing ever retries SMS cancellation, so the row leaks permanently and, for transient Twilio failures, the SMS is still delivered for a cancelled booking. The refactor removed all remaining uses of the Prisma namespace in this file (the deleted code was the last place referencing Prisma.BatchPayload), but the import was kept and even changed from `import type` to a value import. `Prisma` is now an unused import in this module (PrismaPromise is still used), which the repo's lint rules (no-unused-vars) will flag.

This is the second attempt to fix reminders being sent for cancelled/rescheduled bookings — the first fix silently failed in production for an extended period — yet the PR adds no tests covering the new mechanism: setting cancelled=true on cancel/reschedule, the cron cancellation loop (including its all-or-nothing failure behavior when a SendGrid request fails), and the reschedule cancellation in handleNewBooking. Regression coverage around handleCancelBooking and scheduleEmailReminders would materially reduce the risk of another silent failure of this fix.
