true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, releases it, and then acquires the write lock at line 48 — but never re-checks the cache once the write lock is held. When multiple requests race before the cache is first populated (e.g. at startup), each one sequentially re-opens and re-parses assets-manifest.json and overwrites the cache, defeating most of the benefit of the fix. Worse, if goroutine B populates the cache successfully and goroutine A's redundant re-read then fails (file removed during startup, transient I/O error), line 69 stores nil over the valid cache and A returns an error to its caller even though assets were already loaded. Add a second nil check after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking) so only the first caller performs the load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate the cache. The candidate describes the same incomplete double-checked locking issue and adds potential consequences.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under a read lock, releases it, and then acquires the write lock at line 48 — but never re-checks the cache once the write lock is held. When multiple requests race before the cache is first populated (e.g. at startup), each one sequentially re-opens and re-parses assets-manifest.json and overwrites the cache, defeating most of the benefit of the fix. Worse, if goroutine B populates the cache successfully and goroutine A's redundant re-read then fails (file removed during startup, transient I/O error), line 69 stores nil over the valid cache and A returns an error to its caller even though assets were already loaded. Add a second nil check after acquiring the write lock (standard double-checked locking) so only the first caller performs the load.
true_positives.reasoning: Although framed around the missing cache re-check, the candidate explicitly identifies that a failed fetch stores nil at line 69 and overwrites a previously valid cache entry, matching the golden comment's underlying error-handling bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across file (and potential network) I/O

The write lock is taken at line 48 and held via defer for the entire remainder of GetWebAssets, which includes the assets-manifest.json read at line 60 and — if the cdn variable at line 54 is ever set to a non-empty value as the comment suggests — a CDN HTTP fetch via http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout. While one caller performs that I/O, every other goroutine calling GetWebAssets blocks on the mutex, including callers that would have been satisfied by the already-populated cache; in dev mode (where the cache is never consulted) this serializes every call. Consider performing the load outside the critical section and taking the write lock only to publish the result, combined with the double-check described above.

No regression test for the data race being fixed

This PR exists to fix a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache, but it adds no test that would catch a regression. A test that invokes GetWebAssets concurrently from multiple goroutines (with cfg.Env != setting.Dev so the cache path is exercised) and is run under `go test -race` would fail before this change and pass after it. Without such a test, a future refactor of this function can silently reintroduce the unsynchronized access, and CI will not notice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID slices, on every batch

The new batched cleanup logs routine progress at Error level in six places (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579): "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Annotations to clean by count", "cleaned annotations by count", "Tags to clean", and "cleaned tags". These fire unconditionally for every batch of every annotation type on every cleanup run — including steady-state runs where count is 0 and nothing was deleted — and each line embeds the complete "ids" slice, whose length is the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (the PR's own test uses 32767, so a single log line can contain tens of thousands of IDs). The cleanup job also now runs every minute (see cleanup.go), so this produces a constant stream of multi-kilobyte Error log lines, which will swamp error logs and trip any alerting based on error-level log volume. Lines 534/554/576 also log "err", err where err is nil by construction. These look like debugging leftovers; they should be demoted to Debug (and the ids/cond fields dropped or truncated) before merging.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify routine debugging or progress information being logged at Error level, polluting production error logs, and recommend lowering the log level. The candidate adds specifics about frequency and payload size but describes the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs

The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the stated purpose of the PR (splitting the annotation cleanup DELETE to avoid MySQL deadlocks) and is not mentioned in the description. It makes every cleanup job run 10x more often — temp file cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, and query history (the last of which runs several DELETE/count queries each cycle) — multiplying background database and filesystem load for all Grafana instances. If the intent was to let the batched annotation cleanup converge faster, that should be scoped to the annotation job or justified in the PR; otherwise this line looks like a local-testing leftover that should be reverted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute and warn that more frequent cleanup execution increases database load and potential contention. The candidate provides additional context but describes the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Inline ID list for SQLite built with O(n^2) string concatenation

In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback path (used when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999) builds the IN-list string with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all ids. Each iteration reallocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of N IDs costs O(N^2) in bytes copied — with the batch size of 32767 exercised by the new test that is on the order of several GB of copying per batch, and the tag cleanup runs the same path with even more IDs. This runs on every cleanup cycle when a large batch size is configured. Using a strings.Builder (or strings.Join on a pre-converted []string) with strconv.AppendInt would make it linear.

Subtest cleanup registered after data creation; a failure leaves dirty tables and cascades via PK conflicts

In TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, each subtest creates its annotations and runs assertions (which use require, aborting the subtest on failure) before registering t.Cleanup at line 120. Because createTestAnnotations now inserts rows with explicit primary keys (ID: int64(i+1), line 241) and all subtests share the same fakeSQL database, any failure before the cleanup is registered leaves rows behind, and every subsequent subtest then fails with primary-key conflicts on IDs 1..N rather than its actual assertion result, making the real failure hard to diagnose. Registering the t.Cleanup before createTestAnnotations (so tables are truncated even on early failure) avoids the cascade.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` should pass `log` — the logger that was just built with name/kind/method values. As written, anything downstream that uses `klog.FromContext(ctx)` (including the storage and legacy delete calls in this method) logs without the identifying fields, unlike every other method in this file which passes the enriched logger.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that klog.NewContext uses d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, preventing the name, kind, and method fields from propagating to downstream logging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with the object name as the resource label

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name in the position where every other call site in this file passes `options.Kind`. If the third argument is the metric's resource label (as all the kind-based call sites indicate), this creates a Prometheus series per deleted object name — unbounded cardinality that grows with every object — and breaks per-kind aggregation/alerting for the delete method. Use `options.Kind` here.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: Delete passes the object name to recordStorageDuration where other methods pass options.Kind. The candidate adds metric-cardinality consequences but points to the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and are cancelled when the request completes

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming apiserver request context. For server requests, the context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which happens immediately after the dual writer returns its response. The 10-second timeout therefore almost never gets to run: every legacy write races with request teardown and will frequently fail with context.Canceled. Since the failure is only recorded in a metric and never logged, mode 3 silently drops the 'safety' legacy writes it exists to perform, leaving legacy and unified storage permanently diverged with no signal. The goroutine context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (which preserves values like the logger and user) before applying the timeout.

Unified-storage failures are recorded as legacy metric errors (and vice versa in DeleteCollection)

In Create (line 45) and Update (line 129), when `d.Storage` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — the failed unified-storage call is recorded as a legacy error and no storage-side failure is recorded at all. Conversely, in DeleteCollection's goroutine (line 166) the legacy delete-collection result is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(...)`. These metrics misattribute failures to the wrong backend in both directions, which will mislead the dashboards/alerting used to judge whether it is safe to advance to mode 4. The Create/Update error paths should use `recordStorageDuration`, and the DeleteCollection goroutine should use `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy goroutine reuses the request object that unified storage may have mutated and that is being serialized for the response

The goroutine calls `d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, ...)` with the same `runtime.Object` pointer that was just handed to `d.Storage.Create`. k8s-style stores mutate the object passed to Create/Update (setting UID, resourceVersion, generation, timestamps) and typically return that same pointer as `created`. If unified storage does that, the legacy goroutine and the HTTP handler then concurrently mutate and serialize the same object: the legacy store can overwrite unified's resourceVersion/UID on the object being written to the response — a data race and a potentially corrupted response body. Previously the legacy call was synchronous so mutation ordering was controlled; making it async requires passing `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the legacy call (same concern applies to the Update path reusing request-scoped objects).

Unordered async legacy writes can leave legacy permanently stale (lost updates)

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering guarantees. Two quick successive updates to the same object (or a create immediately followed by an update) can be applied to legacy out of order: the goroutine carrying the newer update may finish before the older one, which then overwrites legacy with stale data. Because legacy errors are only counted in a metric and never logged, nothing surfaces this divergence, and the legacy copy — the stated purpose of mode 3 ('just as a safe measure') — can silently remain at an old revision indefinitely. Legacy writes need per-object serialization (e.g. a single ordered worker/queue) and/or resourceVersion-based conflict handling.

Async legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere

In all four write methods the error from the async legacy call is only passed to `recordLegacyDuration`; the previous implementation logged it (e.g. `log.Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`). For a mode whose purpose is keeping legacy as a safety net, a failing safety net with no log entry makes diagnosis impossible — this would also have made the request-context cancellation bug visible in logs. Log the error with object identifiers inside each goroutine.

Mode 3 unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens

The legacy expectations are registered on a testify mock that is shared between the legacy and unified mocks (both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`), and the tests return immediately after the dual-writer call without waiting for the legacy goroutine or calling AssertExpectations. Consequences: (a) the success cases pass even if the legacy call never runs — the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go fails nothing here; (b) because both backends share one mock, the Create error case registers only a 'legacy' expectation and it is actually `Storage.Create` that matches it, so the test's name and setup do not reflect what is exercised. Use separate mocks and wait/assert on the legacy invocation (e.g. require.Eventually) so each backend's call and ordering is genuinely checked.

New mode-3 playlist subtests assert legacy state immediately after asynchronous legacy writes and will be flaky

`doPlaylistTests` performs k8s writes and then immediately reads through the legacy API (`getFromBothAPIs`, the 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' subtest, and the `/api/playlists` list comparisons) expecting both backends to agree. Under mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these cross-backend assertions race the legacy goroutine — they pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling (and fail outright whenever the legacy write is cancelled at request end, per the context bug in dualwriter_mode3.go). The two new mode-3 runs of this shared test need to poll for convergence on the legacy side (e.g. require.Eventually) or use relaxed expectations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in the filtered rule list

In the `rules.map(...)` switch, the 'grafana' branch returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` without the `key={key}` prop that the previous `<GrafanaRuleLoader>` had (the 'datasource' and default branches still set `key`). 'Silence notifications' menu item is shown in the ruler-less list view but clicking it does nothing

Clicking the item therefore toggles state without rendering a drawer or producing a visible effect.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable after the useAllAlertRuleAbilities refactor

Before this change, `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made rules in Mimir federated groups (groups with `source_tenants`) non-editable/non-deletable in the UI. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities(rule.rulerRule, groupIdentifierV2)`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO because the group object is no longer passed in. All existing consumers of `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (e.g. RuleActionsButtons, RulesTable, rule details) will now offer Edit/Delete/Pause for federated rules, and those operations will fail at the ruler API. Pass the group (or an isFederated flag) into useAllRulerRuleAbilities so the check is preserved.

Duplicate/View abilities fall back to Grafana permissions for non-Grafana rules when rule is undefined (skipToken)

When the prom rule is not a Grafana rule, callers pass `skipToken`, and `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` runs with `rule === undefined`. With no rule, `loading` is false, so `MaybeSupported` becomes `AlwaysSupported` and `[AlertRuleAction.Duplicate]` evaluates to `[true, has-grafana-create-permission]` using `getRulesPermissions('grafana')` (same for View with grafana read permission). AlertRuleMenu and RuleActionsButtons OR these abilities with the ruler-based ones, so for a cloud (Mimir/Loki) rule, a user who only has Grafana-managed rule create permission — but not `alert.rules.external:write` — will now see the Duplicate menu item; the actual operation will fail server-side. When the rule is undefined the hook should return all-false abilities instead of evaluating grafana permissions.

Export (modify-export) and pause support dropped for Grafana recording rules in the list view

The ruler-based ability used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` — true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules — to gate `ModifyExport`, `Pause` and `Restore`. The new `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gates these on `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, which is false for recording rules, even though modify-export and pausing are supported for Grafana recording rules elsewhere. Because the list view no longer fetches ruler rules, the OR fallback in AlertRuleMenu can't compensate, so Grafana recording rules lose the Export menu item in the list (and the Pause ability now reports unsupported). Use the recording-inclusive type guard where the ruler version used `grafana.rule`.

Rule view link lost the returnTo parameter

The removed GrafanaRuleLoader built the rule href with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using createReturnTo(); the new GrafanaRuleListItem builds the same URL without `returnTo`. Navigating back from a rule to the list no longer restores the user's previous list location/filter state. Restore the `returnTo` query parameter.

Stale comment about preloading ruler rules after the prefetch was removed

The comment 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX…' and the variable name `cacheAndRulerPreload` still describe ruler preloading, but the `alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', …)` call was removed in this PR. The comment/name is now misleading about what the code does and should be updated.

Shard-splitting path now interpolates every target twice

runShardSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 52), but the already-interpolated targets are then passed via subRequest into runSplitQuery() (line 163), which after this PR also maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (querySplitting.ts line 299). So in the shard path each query is interpolated once per shard-group request plus once at entry. The updated test codifies this: 'Interpolates queries before running' now expects applyTemplateVariables to have been called 5 times for a single-target request (1 + 4 shard sub-requests). Re-running template expansion on already-interpolated text is a known source of query corruption in Grafana: if a variable's value contains '$'-syntax (e.g. a custom variable value containing '${other_var}' or a label value with a '$' token matching another variable), the second pass will expand tokens introduced by the first pass and silently change the query sent to Loki. The new code filters on the raw, uninterpolated expr (lines 50-51) and interpolates afterwards (line 52), so such a query now passes the filter and proceeds with an empty interpolated expr: it is grouped via getSelectorForShardValues(''), triggers a fetchLabelValues call with an empty stream selector, and is ultimately sent to Loki as an empty query, which will return a parse error to the user instead of being silently ignored. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both read the same value, so one increment is silently lost. The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`, but no Microsoft flexbox implementation ever supported that property — IE10's 2012 'tweener' syntax uses `-ms-flex-align` (which the mixin already emits on the previous line). true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that -ms-align-items was never supported by IE/Edge and that the correct legacy Microsoft flexbox property is -ms-flex-align.

Per CSS, floats have no effect on flex items, so the `button { float: right; }` rule inside `.small-action` stops working for any button that is a direct child of the `.small-action` row. Previously that button was pinned to the right edge of the post row; now it will be packed immediately after `.small-action-desc` on the left, because the container has no `justify-content: space-between` and the button has no `margin-left: auto`. If the button is a direct child (as the old float-based layout implies), this is a visible layout regression for small action posts (e.g. undo/expand controls). true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is the full referer URL — browsers throw and the iframe never resizes

Additionally, the referer is interpolated into a single-quoted JS string and html_escape does not escape apostrophes on all Rails versions this repo supports, so a referer containing a raw ' would also break the script.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: using the full referrer URL as postMessage's targetOrigin instead of its origin, preventing delivery of the resize message. RSS feed content is stored as raw, unsanitized HTML — stored XSS on the forum domain

PollFeed takes each feed item's HTML (CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)) and passes it to TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html] (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22). Post#cook returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html posts (app/models/post.rb:133), so `cooked` contains the feed markup verbatim with zero sanitization, and it is rendered unescaped (<%= raw post.cooked %> in app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19, and as cooked HTML in the main app). Any <script> or on* handler in a feed item becomes stored XSS executing on the forum domain for every visitor. The CGI.unescapeHTML makes this worse: the XML parser already decodes entities once, so content the feed author properly escaped (e.g. `<script>` in a code sample) is decoded a second time into live markup — even a fully trusted blog can inject live scripts. Note the import_remote path at least whitelists tags/attributes via Readability; the RSS path sanitizes nothing. Feed content should be run through Sanitize (or an equivalent whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

Server-side fetch follows redirects to any host — SSRF past the embeddable_host check

TopicRetriever#invalid_host? only validates that URI(embed_url).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but TopicEmbed.import_remote fetches with `open(url)` (open-uri), which transparently follows HTTP redirects to arbitrary hosts. An open redirect on the allowed host (e.g. http://blog.example.com/out?u=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data or an intranet address) lets an external requester make the forum server fetch internal URLs; the response is then Readability-parsed and published as a public topic, exfiltrating the content. The fetch layer should validate every redirect target against the allowed host or disable cross-host redirects.

Loading page self-reload fails the controller's referer check — embed gets stuck on 403

The loading page reloads itself every 30s via document.location.reload() so it picks up the topic once the RetrieveTopic job finishes. A programmatic reload sends the iframe's own URL (the /embed/best URL on the forum host) as the Referer, not the embedding page's URL. EmbedController#ensure_embeddable (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:26) compares URI(referer).host to SiteSetting.embeddable_host and raises Discourse::InvalidAccess on mismatch, so the reload gets a 403 and the embed is permanently stuck on an error page instead of showing the newly imported topic. The referer check needs to also accept the forum's own embed URL (or the loading flow needs another mechanism, e.g. message-bus).

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs (//host/path)

The relative-URL rewrite treats any href/src starting with '/' as host-relative: a protocol-relative URL like //cdn.example.com/a.png matches `href.start_with?('/')` and is rewritten to http://blog.example.com/cdn.example.com/a.png, producing a broken link. Protocol-relative URLs are common in feed/article HTML. The check should exclude values starting with '//' (and ideally also absolutize paths that don't start with '/', which are currently left relative and break in the forum context).

URIs that pass the regex but are invalid crash the whole import run

URLs are only validated against /^https?:\/\// before URI(url) is called in absolutize_urls (and open(url) in import_remote). Feed links or embed URLs containing spaces or other characters illegal in URIs (e.g. 'http://example.com/my post.html') pass the regex but raise URI::InvalidURIError here, which is not rescued — in PollFeed this aborts the entire hourly run so no further feed items are imported, and in the RetrieveTopic job it causes repeated sidekiq retries. Validate with URI.parse in a begin/rescue and skip bad items instead of aborting.

ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT + NOT NULL rewrites the entire posts table and blocks writes

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false forces PostgreSQL (< 11) to rewrite every row of the posts table while holding an AccessExclusiveLock. posts is the largest table in a Discourse install, so on any sizable forum this migration blocks all posting/reading for minutes during a deploy. Safer pattern: add the column without a default, backfill in batches, then set the default and the NOT NULL constraint.

Find-then-create race on embed_url unique index aborts concurrent import jobs

import does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and later TopicEmbed.create! inside a transaction. Two concurrent jobs for the same URL (a RetrieveTopic job racing the hourly PollFeed, or two RetrieveTopic jobs for staff, who bypass the redis throttle) both see no existing embed and both build a topic and post; the second create! hits the unique index on topic_embeds.embed_url and raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, failing that job — and in PollFeed, aborting the rest of the feed items. Rescue RecordNotUnique/re-check inside the transaction or use an upsert-style create_or_find.

retrieved_recently? does $redis.setnx(retrieved_key, '1') followed by a separate $redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60). If the process crashes (or expire raises) between the two calls, the key never expires and retrieve() will treat that embed_url as recently retrieved forever — the topic is never fetched. Use a single atomic SET with an EX option (supported by redis-rb) instead of the two-step dance.

This changes the shipped 20131223171005_create_top_topics migration to create_table :top_topics, force: true. Databases that already ran the migration will never re-run it, so the change is a silent no-op there; on fresh or restored setups, force: true will silently DROP and recreate the table (and any data) if it already exists. Released migrations shouldn't be modified — add a new migration instead. The new db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb uses force: true too, carrying the same silent-drop risk.

These specs would still pass if the url/username presence checks were removed entirely. Each gating test should stub all the prior conditions to true so only the condition under test fails.

false_positives.candidate:
Busy times are ignored on date-override days, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the code reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (lines 133-135) and returns before the `busy.every(...)` check at the end of the function is ever evaluated. `busy` contains the host's existing Cal.com bookings and external calendar events, so on any day that has a date override, none of the host's actual commitments block slots. This applies to fixed hosts in round-robin/collective events, to loose hosts (the loose-host loop calls the same function), and to personal events (whose single user counts as fixed). A host who already has a booking or calendar event inside an override window can be double-booked. The early return should only skip the working-hours check; the busy check must still run.

Working-hours check rejects every slot for hosts with multiple windows per day

The new working-hours guard uses `workingHours.find(...)` and returns `false` (slot unavailable) whenever the predicate matches ANY window in which the slot does not fit. Hosts commonly define split availability on a day, e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, which produces two WorkingHours entries with the same days. Any slot is necessarily outside at least one of those windows, so `find` always returns truthy and every slot is rejected. Because checkIfIsAvailable now runs for every fixed host (including the single user of a personal event, and both hosts of collective events), any event whose host has more than one availability window per day becomes completely unbookable on all days. The logic needs to be inverted: reject only when NO window for that day fully contains the slot (e.g. `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`).

Multiple date-override windows on the same date break the availability check

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` predicate returns true (causing the slot to be rejected with `return false`) for the first override on the matching date in which the slot is NOT contained, and find() stops iterating there. With two override windows on the same date (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot at 14:30 is rejected because it is outside the first window, and a slot at 10:30 is rejected because it is outside the second window. Only a single override window per date works correctly. The check needs 'there exists an override on this date that contains the slot' semantics rather than short-circuiting on the first non-containing override.

Override containment check treats partial overlap as available and misses the exact end boundary

The conditions used to decide that a slot is outside an override are `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` and `slotStartTime > overrideEnd` (strict isAfter). Anything else — including a slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside and ends after it — is treated as 'within the override' and the host is considered available, even though part of the slot falls outside the override window. Additionally, a slot starting exactly at the override end fails the strict `isAfter` and is also treated as inside the override. For round-robin events where slots are generated from other hosts' working hours, this lets fixed hosts be booked outside their override window. Availability should require full containment: slotStart >= overrideStart && slotEnd <= overrideEnd.

Timezone-shifted date overrides that cross midnight are silently dropped

The override start/end are shifted by (inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset) and then reduced to hour/minute-of-day via `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`. When the shift pushes the interval across midnight — e.g. a 09:00-17:00 IST override viewed from PST (offset -810 minutes shifts start to 19:30 of the previous day and end to 03:30) — the wrapped startTime (1170) becomes greater than endTime (210) whenever only one side of the interval wraps, and buildSlots silently skips the range (`if (start >= end) continue`). Meanwhile the user's regular working hours for that day were already spliced out of computedLocalAvailability, so the invitee sees the host as fully unavailable that day. Regular working hours handle midnight spanning by splitting the range; overrides need the same treatment.

Override date matching is formatted in the server's local timezone but compared to a UTC date

`dayjs(date.start)` creates a dayjs in the server machine's local timezone, and `.add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` is compared against `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`, where slotStartTime is in UTC mode. On any host not running in UTC (self-hosted instances with a TZ set, dev machines), the two sides of the comparison are rendered in different zones, so an override can be matched against the wrong day near midnight. `dayjs.utc(date.start)` should be used so both sides are in UTC.

Override timezone conversion silently depends on the server timezone when timeZone is absent

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is used to compute the organizer offset, but `timeZone` was added as an optional property on TimeRange, and dayjs.tz with an undefined zone falls back to the machine's local timezone. Any caller of getSlots that passes dateOverrides without a timeZone now gets results that depend on the server's timezone (and differ between UTC production servers and non-UTC dev machines), whereas the previous code did not consult a timezone at all. A deterministic fallback (e.g. `override.timeZone ?? organizerTimeZone`) should be used.

No tests for the round-robin fixed-host scenario or for busy blocking on override days

The PR adds only one test: a personal event viewed from a different timezone. The headline fix — date overrides of a fixed host constraining a round-robin event's slots — has no test. There is also no test that an existing booking or calendar busy time still blocks a slot on a date-override day (which would have caught the regression where the busy check is skipped when a date override matches), and no coverage for hosts with multiple working-hour windows in one day or multiple override windows on one date, both of which the new checkIfIsAvailable logic handles incorrectly.

When a refresh response omits `refresh_token`, the code writes the literal string "refresh_token" into the result. office365calendar then merges this over the stored credential (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and zoomvideo assigns `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` directly, and both persist it. If the sync feature is later disabled, or a provider omits refresh_token in a normal refresh, the credential's real refresh token is permanently replaced with the placeholder and all future refreshes fail with invalid_grant, requiring the user to reconnect.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: when an OAuth refresh response omits refresh_token, the code substitutes the literal string "refresh_token", invalidating the stored credential and breaking subsequent refreshes. The candidate adds details about how the placeholder is persisted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema drops expiry and refresh_token — computed keys collapse and zod strips unknown fields

The schema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`; both evaluate to "[object Object]", so the second overwrites the first, and the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. Because zod strips unknown keys by default, parsing any token response returns only `{ access_token }` — the comments claiming "any property with a number is the expiry" are wrong. Consequences in the sync path: in zoomvideo `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` becomes NaN (which then fails zoomTokenSchema's z.number() on the next read, breaking Zoom entirely), and office365calendar never updates its stored expiry.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same misuse of computed Zod property keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema. The candidate describes key collisions and stripped fields rather than the golden comment's runtime error, but points to the same underlying schema bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. The catch block treats it as a non-'invalid_grant' error and silently returns myGoogleAuth with the old, expired credentials, so every Google Calendar API call for synced users fails with 401s and the credential is never marked invalid.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
refreshOAuthTokens is called with credentialId instead of userId

`refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` is invoked as `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`. The third parameter is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`, so the platform receives a credential row id instead of the Cal.com user id. Since credential ids and user ids overlap numerically, the platform can resolve this to a *different* user and return that user's third-party tokens, which would then be stored on this user's credential — a cross-user token leak. Every other app in this PR passes `credential.userId`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect argument: refreshOAuthTokens receives credentialId instead of userId, causing incorrect user lookups during credential synchronization. The candidate adds a potential security consequence but still describes the same underlying bug.

Additionally, after refreshing and persisting the new token, the jsforce.Connection is created with the OLD `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` instead of `accessTokenParsed.data`, so the fresh token is never actually used.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid webhook payloads throw unhandled 500s instead of 4xx responses

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on any malformed body, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` (line 57) throws on a wrongly encrypted or non-JSON payload; neither is wrapped in try/catch, so callers get an unhandled 500 with a stack trace rather than a 400. The handler also never checks `req.method`, so even a GET with no body hits these throwing paths. The webhook secret comparison at line 25 is also not constant-time.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) throws on invalid payloads without handling, producing 500 errors instead of the expected 400 responses. Additional concerns do not change this direct match.

false_positives.candidate:
prisma is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService

The new code in getClient() calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (the import block at the top only imports jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a `Cannot find name 'prisma'` type-check failure / ReferenceError at runtime, so the build breaks and the Salesforce integration cannot work at all.

Sync-path Response object is persisted as the HubSpot credential key, destroying the stored credential

`refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when credential sync is enabled, but the result is typed/used as `HubspotToken`. In the sync path: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined so `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` sets undefined, and `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes a Response object — i.e. the stored credential key is overwritten with `{"expiryDate": null}`. The user's HubSpot credential (including the refresh token) is permanently wiped and they must reconnect the app.

Zoom refresh passes app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the self-hoster's sync endpoint, but Zoom's app slug everywhere else is "zoom" (see zoomvideo/api/callback.ts which stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new webhook endpoint which looks up `prisma.app` by slug). The platform cannot resolve "zoomvideo" to the Zoom app, so token refresh via the sync endpoint will fail for Zoom. Every other app passes its real slug ("google-calendar", "msteams", "webex", etc.).

axios response shape assumed, but sync path returns a fetch Response

The normal refresh function returns an AxiosResponse (read via `tokenInfo.data`), but `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when sync is enabled, which has no `.data`. `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, so Zoho Bigin token refresh always crashes when credential sync is enabled. The same class of mismatch applies to zohocrm.

axios/fetch response mismatch breaks ZohoCRM refresh when sync is enabled

The wrapped refresh function returns an AxiosResponse, but the sync branch of `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` with no `.data` property. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` therefore throws a TypeError; it is swallowed by `catch (e) { this.log.error(e); }`, leaving `this.accessToken` unset/stale. All subsequent Zoho CRM API calls go out with an empty or expired `Zoho-oauthtoken` header and fail, silently breaking the integration for synced users.

Webex refresh always rejects when credential sync is enabled

Unlike the other apps, webex kept validating with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`, and literal `scope`/`token_type` values. The documented sync-endpoint contract ("response should only contain the access token and expiry date") can never satisfy this schema, so `parsedToken.success` is always false and refresh always rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — Webex is broken whenever credential sync is on.

Lark refresh expects Lark's {code, data} envelope but sync endpoint returns a flat minimal payload

The sync-path response from `refreshOAuthTokens` is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>` and then read as `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, etc. The sync endpoint returns a flat `{access_token, expiry}` payload (per the documented contract in refreshOAuthTokens), so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws (or stores undefined token fields into the credential key). Lark calendar refresh is broken when credential sync is enabled.

findFirst by userId+appId can overwrite the wrong credential for multi-account apps

Cal.com allows a user to connect multiple accounts for the same app (e.g. several Google or Office 365 calendars), producing multiple Credential rows with the same userId and appId. The webhook's `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key with the pushed credentials, so the platform can silently clobber the tokens of a different account than intended. The payload needs an account identifier (e.g. email/external id) to target the correct credential.

Outbound request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication

The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no shared secret, signature, or header (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is only checked on the inbound webhook). The platform endpoint therefore cannot verify the request genuinely comes from its Cal.com instance; anyone who can reach that endpoint can request freshly refreshed third-party OAuth tokens for any user id / app. The implementation should include the shared secret (or an HMAC) so the platform can authenticate the caller.

No tests for the webhook endpoint or the sync refresh paths

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This change adds a new authenticated credential-writing endpoint and rewires token refresh for nine integrations with two divergent code paths (direct provider refresh vs. platform sync endpoint); the response-shape mismatches introduced here (axios vs fetch, GaxiosResponse vs fetch Response) are exactly the kind of regression a small unit/integration test per service would have caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation calls in booking-cancel handler are fire-and-forget

deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder are invoked without await inside the forEach. These calls perform the only state change that now prevents the reminders from being sent: setting cancelled=true (which the cron job relies on to cancel the SendGrid scheduled send) and, for SMS, the Twilio cancel plus DB delete. The previous version of this function collected the reminder deletions and awaited them via Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)); now nothing reminder-related is awaited. On a serverless platform the invocation can be frozen once the response is sent, before these floating promises finish — the cancelled flag is then never persisted, the cron never cancels the SendGrid scheduled send, and the reminder email is still delivered, i.e. the exact bug this PR fixes persists intermittently. Collect the promises and await them before returning.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach, allowing reminder cancellation to remain incomplete. It focuses on booking cancellation rather than all affected paths, but matches the golden issue and consequence.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path neither deletes nor flags the reminder row and has no retry on failure

When immediateDelete is true (used by the reschedule flow in handleNewBooking and by workflow/step deletion in the workflows router), deleteScheduledEmailReminder only posts the cancel to SendGrid and returns — it never deletes the WorkflowReminder row and never sets cancelled=true. Two consequences: (1) if the SendGrid request fails, the catch only logs and nothing retries — the row keeps scheduled=true and cancelled=null, so the old booking's reminder email is still sent (duplicates after a reschedule); (2) in the reschedule flow the stale rows (scheduled=true, referenceId set, cancelled=null) linger in the DB until the cron's past-date deleteMany removes them days later, unlike every other cancellation path which deletes or flags the row. Consider deleting the row (or marking it cancelled as a fallback) even in the immediate path, so a failed SendGrid call is retried by the cron instead of being silently lost.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: the immediateDelete path cancels through SendGrid but leaves the WorkflowReminder database record neither deleted nor marked cancelled. It adds retry-related concerns and does not explicitly mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE call, but the underlying orphaned-record issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the entire cancellation batch for the cron run

The new cancellation block wraps the whole for-loop in a single try/catch. If client.request throws for any one reminder (transient SendGrid error, invalid/already-cancelled batch_id, or SendGrid rejecting a cancel that is too close to the scheduled send time), execution jumps straight to the catch: (a) every remaining reminder in remindersToCancel is skipped for that run, and (b) none of the prisma.workflowReminder.delete calls collected so far actually execute, because they are only awaited after the loop via Promise.all and Prisma promises are lazy (they don't run until awaited). On the next cron run the same rows are re-fetched (still cancelled=true) and the loop aborts again at the same poisoned row, so a single bad reminder can block cancellation of all pending cancelled reminders until its own scheduledDate passes — at which point the first deleteMany in this handler silently drops the row and the email has already been sent. Each loop iteration needs its own try/catch (and each row should be deleted right after its own successful cancel) so one failure doesn't stall the queue.

Deferred-only cancellation still misses reminders cancelled close to their send time

With this PR, cancellation of scheduled emails happens exclusively in this cron job, which runs every 15 minutes and only cancels reminders whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. If a booking is cancelled shortly before a reminder's send time, the next cron run may not happen before SendGrid sends the email, and SendGrid does not allow changing the status of a scheduled send that is about to go out — so the reminder is delivered for a cancelled booking even though the cancellation was recorded in time. Consider using the immediate path (deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true, already used in the reschedule flow) for reminders whose scheduledDate is near (e.g. within the next hour), and deferring only far-future cancellations to the cron. That still avoids the 100-pending-cancellations limit while closing the last-minute gap.

Newly added reschedule reminder-cancellation is fire-and-forget

In the reschedule flow, the loop that cancels the original booking's workflow reminders calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...) without awaiting them, and the surrounding try/catch cannot observe their completion (the functions also swallow their own errors). If the serverless invocation is frozen after the response is sent before these promises finish, the original booking's SendGrid batches are never cancelled while the new booking's reminders are scheduled — so both old and new reminders fire, the duplicate-reminder bug for rescheduled bookings this PR is meant to fix. Await these calls.

requestReschedule: reminder cancellation no longer awaited

This handler previously awaited the reminder cleanup via `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`; the refactor removed that and now calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder without await inside forEach. The cancelled flag / row deletion these calls perform is the only thing preventing reminders for the cancelled booking from being sent, so for reliability they should be collected and awaited rather than left floating in a serverless handler.

WorkflowReminder row is leaked when Twilio cancel fails

In deleteScheduledSMSReminder, if twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId) throws (transient error, or the message was already sent), the catch skips the prisma.workflowReminder.delete call. The row is then left behind with scheduled=true and cancelled unset, and — unlike the email path, which flags rows for the cron to retry — nothing ever retries SMS cancellation, so the row leaks permanently and, for transient Twilio failures, the SMS is still delivered for a cancelled booking. Previously the callers deleted these rows in an awaited Promise.all regardless of the Twilio result. Delete the row even when the Twilio cancel fails (or add a retry path).

Prisma import is no longer used

The refactor removed all remaining uses of the Prisma namespace in this file (the deleted code was the last place referencing Prisma.BatchPayload), but the import was kept and even changed from `import type` to a value import. `Prisma` is now an unused import in this module (PrismaPromise is still used), which the repo's lint rules (no-unused-vars) will flag.

No tests for the reworked reminder-cancellation pipeline

This is the second attempt to fix reminders being sent for cancelled/rescheduled bookings — the first fix silently failed in production for an extended period — yet the PR adds no tests covering the new mechanism: setting cancelled=true on cancel/reschedule, the cron cancellation loop (including its all-or-nothing failure behavior when a SendGrid request fails), and the reschedule cancellation in handleNewBooking. Regression coverage around handleCancelBooking and scheduleEmailReminders would materially reduce the risk of another silent failure of this fix.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest dedupe and blacklist checks are case-sensitive

uniqueGuests filters with `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist entries are lowercased but the incoming guest string is not, so `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entirely. Likewise `Existing@Email.com` is not recognized as matching an existing attendee `existing@email.com`, so a duplicate Attendee row is created (the client-side uniqueness refine has the same case-sensitivity problem). Normalize case (and trim whitespace) on the input before comparing.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same blacklist bypass: blacklist entries are lowercased while incoming guest emails are not, so uppercase characters evade the includes check. The additional deduplication concern does not change this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team permission check uses && instead of ||, rejecting team admins

The authorization check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. isTeamAdmin already matches memberships with role ADMIN or OWNER, so AND-ing it with isTeamOwner makes the whole expression equivalent to "user is team owner". Team admins — whom the variable name and the feature intend to allow — will always fail this check and hit the FORBIDDEN branch, so they cannot add guests to team bookings. The `&&` should be `||`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same authorization bug: using && between the team admin and owner checks incorrectly requires both, whereas || should allow either role. The candidate adds detail about the effect on team admins without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type settings that disable standard emails

Every other send* function in this file accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails when eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail is set (event types can disable standard emails, e.g. for custom workflows/platform customers). sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata parameter and addGuests.handler doesn't pass one, so organizers and attendees of event types with standard emails disabled will still receive "Guests Added" and booking-confirmation emails whenever a guest is added, breaking that contract. Thread eventTypeMetadata through and honor the disable flags.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor event-type metadata flags disabling standard host/attendee emails, causing emails to be sent despite those settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add guests, triggering organizer-branded emails to arbitrary addresses

The handler authorizes the request when `isAttendee` is true — any person whose email happens to be on the booking can call viewer.bookings.addGuests with arbitrary addresses. Each call sends an AttendeeScheduledEmail "from" the organizer (replyTo the organizer) to the new addresses plus a notification to every existing attendee. A malicious attendee can therefore spam third parties using the organizer's identity and the booking's legitimacy, with no consent from the organizer and no cap on guests per call. If attendee-initiated guest additions are intentional, this needs rate limiting and sending from the attendee's identity; otherwise the endpoint should be restricted to the organizer and team admins/owners.

Calendar update uses the requester's credentials, not the organizer's, after attendees are already written

`eventManager` is built from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person making the request — but the calendar event being updated lives on the organizer's calendar (booking.user, which is already fetched with credentials in the booking query but never used). When a team owner/admin or an attendee adds guests, EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees searches the requester's credentials for one matching booking.references, which is either missing (throws) or belongs to the wrong user. Because prisma.booking.update has already created the Attendee rows before this call and the call is not wrapped in error handling, the mutation then returns an error even though the guests were persisted: the user sees "unable to add guests", the organizer's calendar event is never updated with the new attendees, and retrying fails with "emails_must_be_unique_valid" because the attendees already exist. Use the organizer's credentials and make the flow failure-safe (e.g., update the calendar before committing, or handle errors so the user is not told the operation failed when it half-succeeded).

No check on booking status or date before adding guests

After loading the booking, the handler never checks booking.status or the booking time, so guests can be added to CANCELLED, REJECTED, PENDING or past bookings. This is reachable from the UI for past confirmed bookings (BookingListItem renders the Edit → "Additional guests" action for `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed`) and via direct API calls for cancelled/rejected ones. Adding a guest to a cancelled booking emails them an AttendeeScheduledEmail with a CONFIRMED ics for an event that no longer exists and permanently attaches attendees to a dead booking. Reject non-ACCEPTED and past bookings before creating attendees.

Adding guests to seated events bypasses seat reservation logic

For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be created together with a BookingSeat record (the handleSeats flow) so that seat availability is counted and the attendee can later cancel/reschedule their seat. This handler blindly creates plain Attendee rows via createMany for any event type, so for seated events the new guests consume no seat — the slot can be overbooked through the normal booking flow afterwards — and the guests have no seat reference for seat-based operations. The handler should either reject seated event types or route through the seat-booking logic.

New guests are stored with the organizer's timeZone and locale

guestsFullDetails sets `timeZone: organizer.timeZone` and `locale: organizer.locale` for every added guest. The AttendeeScheduledEmail sent to those guests renders the meeting time in the attendee's stored timezone — which is actually the organizer's — so guests in other timezones see a wrong local time presented as theirs, and the attendee record permanently carries the wrong timezone/locale (affecting reminders and future emails too). Consider storing a neutral value or making clear whose timezone is displayed.

No limit on number of guests per request

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no .max(), and each call sends an email to every existing attendee plus every new guest, and performs a calendar update. A single request can add hundreds of guests, fanning out hundreds of emails and a large calendar payload — an abuse and performance footgun even for a legitimate organizer. Add a sane .max() on the array and consider a per-booking total guest limit.

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that performs a non-trivial permission matrix (organizer vs team admin vs team owner vs attendee vs stranger), dedupes against existing attendees and a blacklist, writes Attendee rows, updates calendars and sends emails, but adds no unit or integration tests. The permission matrix, duplicate/blacklist filtering, seated-event handling and cancelled-booking behavior are exactly where this implementation has defects; tests covering those cases should be added before merging.

uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code redemption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The login flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then writes the updated array back in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent sign-in requests presenting the same backup code can both decrypt and pass `indexOf` before either update commits, so a code intended to be single-use can be redeemed twice. Use a transaction with a conditional update (or a per-code consumed flag updated atomically) so only one request can consume a given code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent login requests can read and validate the same backup code before either writes the updated codes, allowing a single-use code to be redeemed more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login can skip password verification entirely

In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password check at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the new backup-code branch at line 131 verifies only the backup code. A crafted request to the credentials callback containing a valid `backupCode` together with any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips `verifyPassword` and is authenticated solely by the backup code — a static, 40-bit secret that users store in files/notes. Backup codes are meant to substitute for the authenticator as the second factor, not to replace the password, so a leaked backup code alone yields full account access. The password should be verified (when the user has one) before accepting a backup code, or the flow branching should be keyed off the presence of `backupCode` instead of piggybacking on the `totpCode` gate.

missing_backup_codes message directs users to a settings option that does not exist

The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes outside the initial 2FA setup. Every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped has `backupCodes = null`; if they lose their authenticator and use the new "Lost access" link at login, they hit `MissingBackupCodes` and are told to do something impossible — they cannot log in to reach settings, and even in settings there is no regeneration option. These users are effectively locked out (admin intervention required). Either add a regeneration flow or change the message.

No test exercises the actual backup-code authentication behavior

The only test additions assert that the download/copy/close buttons render on the post-enable screen. Nothing tests the security-critical behavior of the feature: logging in with a backup code, that a redeemed code is invalidated and cannot be reused, that the password is still required alongside a backup code (see the related finding on password skipping), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The added TODO comment ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the unchecked PR checklist item concede this. For an authentication feature, the login-with-backup-code and single-use-invalidation paths should be covered before merge.

Consumed backup codes are nulled instead of removed

After a successful redemption the code does `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts the array, so the stored value permanently accumulates null placeholders (e.g. `[null, null, "abc123...", ...]`). Single-use still works because `indexOf` no longer matches the redeemed string, but the stored blob grows with junk entries and reveals exactly how many codes have been used. Splice the element out (or filter nulls) before re-encrypting.

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashing

Backup codes are stored via `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`. Unlike the TOTP secret, the stored codes are never read back for display — the one-time display uses the in-memory values returned by this same endpoint, and login/disable only need an equality check — so they could be stored as one-way hashes (like passwords). As implemented, anyone who obtains both the database and the encryption key recovers every user's unused backup codes in cleartext.

Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step loses the codes with no recovery path

The backup codes are shown exactly once on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step, and only the explicit Close button calls `onEnable()`. If the user dismisses the dialog at this step in any other way (ESC key or the dialog's close control, which fire `onOpenChange`), the modal closes without `onEnable` being called and the codes — which exist only in this component's React state — can never be displayed or regenerated again. The user's only recourse is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Consider intercepting dismissal on this step with a warning, or providing a way to regenerate codes later.

Copy button shows a success toast even when the clipboard write fails

The copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without awaiting or catching it, then immediately fires `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")`. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied, `writeText` rejects (an unhandled promise rejection) while the user is told the codes were copied — they may close the dialog believing they have codes they don't. Await the promise and only show the success toast on fulfillment, with an error toast on rejection.

Backup codes unusable in the SAML/Google TOTP login flow

When a user with 2FA logs in via Google/SAML they are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` (`totpEmail` set), and in that state the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only offers Cancel — there is no "Lost access" option, so these users cannot enter a backup code even though the credentials provider would accept one. Accounts that enabled 2FA and later moved to an identity-provider login (e.g. after linking Google, which nulls the password) have no self-service recovery path if they lose their authenticator.

Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from keyboard navigation in every `PasswordField` across the app, while it keeps only an sr-only label. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reach the control to verify what they typed. If the goal was to streamline tab order, this trades away an accessibility affordance; consider leaving it focusable.

false_positives.candidate:
Crash when location is Google Meet and destinationCalendar is empty

In `EventManager.create()` the new code does `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then immediately reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` in `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")`. When the event has no destination calendar (e.g. organizer and event type both have none, which `handleNewBooking` now represents as `null`), `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` and accessing `.integration` throws a TypeError, failing the whole booking. The previous code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and safely fell back to Cal Video in exactly this scenario — this is the very fallback the comment describes ('Google Meet selected w/o a Google Cal'). Needs `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

Reschedule only deletes the first old calendar event, leaving stale events on other hosts' calendars

In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, when `newBookingId` is set (reschedule), the cleanup of the old booking's calendar events uses `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))` — a single reference. Now that this PR creates one `_calendar` reference per collective-event host, the old booking can have several calendar references, and only the first host's old event is deleted; the other hosts keep the stale pre-reschedule event on their calendars. This should iterate over all old calendar references (filter) and delete each with its own credentialId/externalCalendarId.

Cancelling all remaining recurring bookings only deletes the first calendar reference per booking

The recurring-cancel branch inside the new per-reference loop still does `const bookingRef = updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` and deletes only that one event, and it iterates only `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's). With multiple hosts, each updated booking now has several `_calendar` references (one per host credential), so the other hosts' recurring instances are never deleted. Additionally, because this whole block is now nested inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`, the entire delete-across-all-credentials routine runs once per reference, issuing duplicate delete calls for the same events.

Confirming a collective booking still builds evt with a single destination calendar

For bookings requiring confirmation, calendar events are created at confirmation time via `handleConfirmation`/`EventManager.create(evt)`, but the `evt` built here sets `destinationCalendar` to only `[booking.destinationCalendar]` or `[user.destinationCalendar]` — the organizer's single calendar. The per-host destination calendars of the other collective hosts are never added, so confirming a collective opt-in booking still only creates the event on the organizer's calendar — the exact bug this PR sets out to fix remains in the confirmation path. The same gap exists in the payment-success flows (`packages/features/ee/payments/api/webhook.ts` and `paypal-webhook.ts`), which also build `evt` with only the booking/organizer destination calendar before calling `eventManager.create(evt)`.

updateLocation creates new references without externalCalendarId/credentialId

In `updateLocation`, `referencesToCreate` now uses `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but these results come from `updateAllCalendarEvents` → `CalendarManager.updateEvent`, whose returned `EventResult` never sets `externalId` or `credentialId`. Previously these were populated from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`/`?.credentialId`. `editLocation.handler` then persists these references (`references: { create: updatedResult.referencesToCreate }`), so after a location edit the new references lack the credential/calendar ids that later update/delete flows depend on.

Reschedule-request deletes calendar events with the organizer's credential instead of each reference's credential

Calendar cleanup here builds `credentialsMap` from the requesting user's credentials keyed by type, then for every booking reference calls `getCalendar(credentialsMap.get(bookingRef.type))` and deletes `bookingRef.uid`. With this PR, collective bookings have references pointing at OTHER hosts' credentials/calendars; deleting those events with the organizer's credential of the same app type will not find the event (different account), so the other hosts' calendar events survive a reschedule request. The per-reference `credentialId` (now stored thanks to this PR) should be used to load the correct credential, as done in `handleCancelBooking`.

Hangout-link patch uses possibly-undefined calendarId after primary fallback

In `createEvent`, the insert uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that writes the hangout link into the description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` directly. When no destination calendar matches the credential (the "primary" fallback path), `selectedCalendar` is `undefined`, so the patch targets `calendars/undefined/...` and the event description never gets the Meet link. Previously `selectedCalendar` was always at least "primary".

loadUsers refactor drops organization.slug from dynamic booking user query

The rewritten `loadUsers` for the dynamic (no eventTypeId) path selects `...userSelect.select, credentials: true, metadata: true` but no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` that the old query included. Any downstream code reading `user.organization?.slug` for dynamic collective bookings (org context/branding/URLs) will now get `undefined`. This change is also unrelated to the destinationCalendar fix.

destinationCalendar falls back to null here but [] everywhere else, and team calendars are silently dropped when null

The new evt initializer uses `: null` when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar, while every other call site in this PR (confirm, cancel, payment webhooks, bookingReminder, etc.) uses `[]`. This makes the webhook payload shape inconsistent (BOOKING_CREATED/BOOKING_REQUESTED send `destinationCalendar: null`, BOOKING_REJECTED sends `[]`), which consumers must special-case — the e2e expectations updated in this PR encode exactly that inconsistency. Additionally, the subsequent `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when the value is null, so for a collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar, the other hosts' calendars are silently discarded.
