true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns deletion failures into unhandled rejections

The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` was changed to `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`, but `forEach` does not collect or return the promises produced by an async callback. The `try { ... } catch` block wrapping the loop (lines 124–139) can therefore no longer catch anything: any synchronous throw that the catch previously handled (e.g. a CalendarService constructor error from `new CalendarService(credential)` inside `getCalendar`) and any rejection from the dynamic import, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` now escapes as an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes Node ≥15 server processes by default and never reaches the `logger.error` path. Additionally, because the callback suspends at the first `await getCalendar(...)`, the `deleteEvent` calls are not even initiated before the function moves on to send the reschedule email and return `true`; in a serverless environment the function can finish (and be frozen) before the calendar/video deletions ever run, leaving stale events on users' calendars while the booking is already marked CANCELLED. Fix by replacing the forEach with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unhandled import-failure concern: the await inside an async forEach callback is not protected by the surrounding try/catch. Its proposed fix makes those rejections catchable, addressing the golden comment despite also discussing broader deletion and sequencing issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns deletion failures into unhandled rejections

Same issue as in packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts: the `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` loop (lines 124–139) discards the promises from its async callback, so the enclosing `try/catch` can no longer catch errors that it previously caught synchronously (e.g. CalendarService constructor failures), and every failure — dynamic import rejection, `calendar.deleteEvent` rejection, `deleteMeeting` rejection — becomes an unhandled promise rejection that bypasses the `logger.error` handling and can crash the Node process. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and return `true` without waiting for any calendar or video deletion to complete; because the callback now suspends at `await getCalendar(...)` before `deleteEvent` is even invoked, the deletions may never start if the serverless invocation ends with the response, leaving stale events on external calendars for a booking already marked CANCELLED. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try.

requestReschedule: deletions are fire-and-forget; failures are now unhandled rejections instead of thrown errors

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` discards all async callback results. Before this change a synchronous failure in `getCalendar` (e.g. a CalendarService constructor throwing) propagated out of the mutation and produced a visible error; now it, and any dynamic-import rejection, becomes an unhandled promise rejection (a crash risk on Node ≥15). Also, since the callback suspends at `await getCalendar` before calling `deleteEvent`, the calendar/video deletions are not even started before the reschedule email is sent and the mutation returns — if the serverless function is frozen after responding, the old event is never removed from the external calendar/meeting provider even though the booking was already marked cancelled and rescheduled. The loop should be `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (ideally with per-item `.catch` logging) so deletions complete and errors are handled before responding.

getCalendarCredentials now embeds an unawaited Promise in the `calendar` field and discards promises for non-calendar variants

`getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function but now calls the newly-async `getCalendar(credential)` without awaiting it, so the returned objects carry `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` where callers previously received `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` (updated in this PR) awaits that field; any other consumer of this exported helper that touches `item.calendar` synchronously will now operate on a Promise instead of a Calendar and break at runtime, and the `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>` contract changed silently. Additionally, `getCalendar(credential)` is invoked before the `app.variant === "calendar"` check, so for non-calendar-variant apps the promise is created and immediately discarded — a rejection of that dynamic import would be an unhandled rejection. Make the function async, resolve with `Promise.all`, and only call `getCalendar` for credentials that are actually returned.

Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so all apps are still loaded on module evaluation

The object literal evaluates each `import("./applecalendar")` etc. immediately when `packages/app-store/index.ts` is first imported, so every consumer of `@calcom/app-store` still triggers loading all 28 app bundles — just asynchronously instead of synchronously. Any code path that needs a single app (e.g. `getCalendar` for one credential type) pays the module-loading cost for all of them, so the change adds asynchrony without delivering the lazy-loading/startup benefit the PR title implies, and on serverless cold starts everything is still fetched and evaluated. If per-app lazy loading is the goal, store thunks or use lazy getters (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and only invoke the one that is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_basic relies on a fixed 0.1s sleep for the flusher thread to produce

The newly added 'step.poll(); time.sleep(0.1)' before step.join() is a timing race: the test asserts exactly one produced message, but the background flusher thread must observe current_drift, call flush_segments against real Redis, and append the message within that wall-clock window. join() sets stopped.value before waiting, so a flush that hasn't happened by then will never occur. On a loaded or slow CI runner where the thread isn't scheduled within 100ms, '(msg,) = messages' will fail intermittently. A poll/wait loop on len(messages) with a timeout would make this deterministic.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment says time.sleep is monkeypatched to return immediately, so the sleep(0.1) does not wait at all. The candidate treats the sleep as a real 0.1s wait that may be too short on a slow runner. Both concern the same line and the flusher not producing in time, but the candidate misses the key point about the monkeypatch. It does flag the same unreliable wait, so this is a partial match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires

In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes breaks out entirely when the deadline is exhausted, so any processes after the one being waited on are never sent terminate(). The previous single-process implementation always called process.terminate() after the wait loop, guaranteeing the old flusher was killed at the deadline. With multiple processes, if an earlier process consumes the remaining time (e.g. it is blocked in a Kafka future.result() wait), the later processes are left running. Since close() deliberately does not stop flushers and join() is the only shutdown point, on a rebalance the leftover processes can overlap with the newly created SpanFlusher's processes for the same shards, causing two flushers to flush the same shard queues concurrently (duplicate segments produced to the buffered-segments topic), and a process hung in produce can leak indefinitely. After the while-wait, terminate() should be called for every remaining process rather than breaking.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue: when the deadline expires, the loop in join() breaks and the remaining flusher processes never get terminate() called, so they can keep running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
max_processes=0 is silently treated as 'one process per shard', negative values disable flushing

self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) conflates an explicit 0 with None: an operator passing --flusher-processes 0 (the click option accepts any int, no range validation) gets 0 or len(shards), i.e. the maximum fan-out of one process per shard instead of zero/one. Conversely a negative value survives the 'or' (truthy), making num_processes = min(negative, shards) negative, so range(num_processes) is empty and no flusher process is created at all — the consumer would keep writing spans to Redis with nothing ever flushing them, with no error surfaced. Consider explicit validation (e.g. click.IntRange(1, ...)) and treating only None as unset.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code left over from the refactor

SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere — restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive, which calls _create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards) directly. The unused method suggests a per-shard restart granularity that does not exist (restarting always recreates the whole process and all its shards), which is misleading for future maintainers. It should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs error_ids with nodestore results positionally, which is not order-safe

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, and then builds events via `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id and does not guarantee that `.values()` comes back in the same order as the requested `node_ids` (and missing keys may be omitted or set to `None`, shifting subsequent pairs). As a result, the `id` recorded on each `ErrorEvent` can be paired with a different event's data. Today the downstream log generation only reads `title`/`message`/`timestamp` (which come from the same data object), so the user-facing impact is currently limited to the latent `id` field being wrong, but the pairing should be done by iterating the node ids and looking up `events[node_id]` instead of relying on positional zip.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug. The code zips error_ids with get_multi's dict values, which assumes the values come back in input order. Missing entries can also shift the alignment, so event data ends up paired with the wrong ID.

In the default attribute view (no search entered), `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` are still rendered, which defeats the purpose of the hidden list. true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

The new matcher is supposed to assert that an access-token ID like "onrtac:<uuid>" carries the expected grant shortcut. In the 6-char prefix the grant shortcut sits at indexes 4-5 (2 chars session type + 2 chars token type + 2 chars grant type), but the code reads items[0].substring(3, 5), i.e. the second token-type character plus the first grant character. On top of that the condition is inverted: it returns false (no match) when the extracted text EQUALS expectedGrantShortcut, so a token with the wrong grant type is always accepted and expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken now assert nothing about the grant. false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing custom OAuth2 grant type providers at server startup

Adding an abstract method to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface means any existing third-party/custom grant-type provider compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError as soon as getShortcut() is invoked on it. That invocation happens eagerly for every registered grant factory in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit(), i.e. during server boot, so upgrading with an existing custom grant provider deployed makes Keycloak fail to start with an obscure error. A default method (for example returning the "na"/unknown shortcut, or deriving a shortcut from the provider id) would keep existing implementations working.

Only the standard token-exchange provider records the grant type; other exchange flows mint tokens with "na" grant

Constants.GRANT_TYPE is set on the client session context only in StandardTokenExchangeProvider. The legacy (V1) token exchange provider and the other V2 exchange providers (subject impersonation, federated) create access tokens through the same TokenManager paths without ever setting this attribute, so access tokens they issue are encoded with the "na" (unknown) grant shortcut instead of "te". Since a stated motivation of this PR is to reliably know the grant type for token-exchange use cases (#37117), the signal will be missing/misleading for those exchange flows.

Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed after successful use

When a user's recovery codes live in a user-storage provider (the capability this PR adds), a successfully used code is never invalidated. For locally stored codes, single-use semantics are enforced inside RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid(), which removes the used code from the stored credential. In the federated path, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid() calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...), which delegates to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid(), and the framework performs no consumption step afterwards. The PR's own reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) only compares the presented code against the stored list and never removes it. Consequences: every recovery code remains valid indefinitely, breaking the one-time-use guarantee of the feature; RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() never becomes true, so the user is never forced to regenerate codes and the login form always asks for code #1; and even if a storage did consume codes itself, the cleanup call authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) operates on Keycloak's local credential store and cannot remove a credential living in user storage. The feature needs a consumption/update mechanism for federated credentials (e.g., writing the reduced code list back through CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential after a successful validation) or the limitation must be explicitly handled.

Plaintext recovery codes are pushed to user storage while local storage keeps only hashes

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and sends them to the user storage via a UserCredentialModel. When the same credential is stored locally, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues() hashes every code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode() so only hashes are persisted (verification is done with verifyRecoveryCodeInput against the hash). Unlike OTP secrets — which an external store genuinely needs in clear text to compute TOTP — recovery-code verification can be performed by hashing the presented code, so there is no technical need to hand the raw codes to the user storage. As implemented, any external user storage that opts into recovery codes ends up holding every user's recovery codes in clear text (and the codes transit in clear through CredentialInput.getChallengeResponse()), so a read-breach of that store, its backups, or its logs exposes all of a user's recovery codes. Consider sending hashed codes to the storage and documenting that storages should hash the presented code in isValid(), matching the local storage security posture.

New recovery-keys test never verifies single-use semantics

testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin performs only one successful login with one recovery code. It never attempts to reuse the same code, never checks that the remaining-code count decreases, and never exercises the all-codes-used path (credential removal and re-adding the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action). Because of this, the test passes even though recovery codes stored in user storage are currently reusable after a successful login — the core security property of the feature is unverified. The test should at minimum assert that a second login attempt with the same code fails and that a subsequent login requests a different code number.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.

After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
CAUTION overstates when the rolling-updates feature must be enabled

The new CAUTION says: "While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the Keycloak Operator will fail." Read literally this tells every reader that any deployment without the preview feature will break, but that is only true when an explicit update strategy is configured. With the default (unset) `spec.update.strategy` the Operator mimics 26.1 behavior and never invokes the update-compatibility command, so it works fine without the feature — this PR's own UpgradeTest demonstrates it: `createInitialDeployment` returns early for the null strategy without enabling `rolling-updates`, and `testCacheMaxCount(null)` still expects a successful rolling-upgrade status. The statement should be scoped (e.g., "must be enabled when configuring `spec.update.strategy`"), otherwise users on the default strategy may wrongly conclude they must enable a preview feature to keep the Operator working.

New and changed update-compatibility exit codes are never asserted

This PR introduces a new exit code (FEATURE_DISABLED = 4, returned when `rolling-updates` is not enabled) and changes the recreate exit code from 4 to 3 in CompatibilityResult, and the update-compatibility guide explicitly tells users to build automation around these exit codes rather than log output. However, no test verifies them: `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr message (line 49) and never checks that the process exits with code 4, and `testWrongVersions`/`testCompatible` assert messages but never assert exit code 3 (recreate required) or 0 (rolling possible) for the `check` command. A future regression that swaps or drops these exit codes — the tool's documented scripting contract — would pass the test suite unnoticed. Please add exitCode assertions to these tests.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting any client throws UnsupportedOperationException when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener (AdminPermissions.java:90-91) handles every ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). With the v2 feature on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose new clients() override now returns ClientPermissionsV2, and ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The new guard added to the listener checks Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (v1), which is also enabled whenever v2 is enabled (v2 presupposes v1), so it does not protect this path. Provider events are published synchronously inside the transaction, so the exception propagates out of the client-removal call, rolls back the transaction and returns a 500 — deleting a client (and any realm teardown that removes clients) is broken under v2. Before this PR the event was dispatched to the v1 ClientPermissions implementation, which successfully removed the client's v2 authorization resources (they live on the same admin-permissions resource server, named by client id), so this is a regression introduced by the clients() override. Either implement the disable/cleanup path in ClientPermissionsV2 or skip this event for v2 in the listener. None of the added tests exercise deleting a client with v2 enabled, which is why this is not caught.

canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles drop the manage/admin-role fallback, denying legitimate admins

The v1 ClientPermissions implementations of canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles and canMapClientScopeRoles all start with `if (canManage(client)) return true;`, i.e. a caller with the manage-clients admin role (or manage permission on the client) may map roles. The new ClientPermissionsV2 overrides (lines 91-103) only evaluate the FGAP MAP_ROLES / MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE / MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE permissions. Consequence: as soon as the v2 feature flag is enabled, a realm admin holding the manage-clients role but no FGAP policies gets 403 from RoleMapperResource.addClientRoleMapping, addComposites, etc. — in every realm, including realms that never opted into admin permissions, because hasPermission() returns false when the realm has no admin-permissions resource server (root.realmResourceServer() == null). Note that AdminPermissions.evaluator() selects MgmtPermissionsV2 based on the profile flag alone, not on realm opt-in. Add `if (canManage(client)) return true;` to the three methods for parity with v1 and with users v2.

getResourceName resolves Users resources to the user's username and labels the all-users resource "All users", but nothing handles the new Clients type. Permission representations for client resources therefore fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never populated for resources created by getOrCreateResource, so the admin API/console shows a null/empty name (or the raw internal client UUID) instead of the clientId, and the all-clients resource gets no friendly label analogous to "All users". Add a Clients branch that resolves ClientModel.getClientId() and an "All clients" label for the type resource.

The newly added javadoc for the void methods requireView() (line 96) and requireViewClientScopes() (line 101) says "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true" — copied from the can* methods; these methods return nothing and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails. In addition, the repeated "For V2 only: Also if the caller has a permission to <scope> for all clients" notes are inaccurate: the v2 implementation checks the specific client's resource first and only falls back to the all-clients resource when no client-specific resource exists, so a client-specific grant (not just an all-clients grant) also satisfies the check. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() evaluates and returns Resource.getId() instead of the group id (resource name)

In the V2 schema, per-group authorization resources are stored with the group id as the resource *name* (AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource -> resolveGroup returns group.getId()). The callback passes groupResource.getId() (the Resource entity UUID) to hasPermission, which looks it up with resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) — that never matches, so evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource instead of each group's own resource, and per-group view-members/manage-members permissions are never detected. AdminPermissions.registerListener handles GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent by calling management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) whenever the admin-fine-grained-authz (v1) feature is enabled. Before this PR, MgmtPermissionsV2 inherited groups() from MgmtPermissions and returned the v1 GroupPermissions, whose setPermissionsEnabled was a harmless no-op against a v2 realm; now MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() returns GroupPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

BuildIndex now only locks cacheMu for the final cache insert, and nothing prevents two goroutines from building the same NamespacedResource concurrently: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex checks GetIndex and then builds outside any lock (its own TODO acknowledges this), so two simultaneous Search requests, or a watch event racing a search, for a namespace that was skipped at startup (below InitMinCount) or newly created will both call BuildIndex. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both call bleve.New on the same directory, so one fails with a store-lock/already-exists error that is surfaced to the user even though nothing is actually wrong; for in-memory indexes one fully built index is silently discarded by the last cache write and IndexTenants is double-counted. The previous whole-function mutex at least serialized these duplicate builds. A per-key lock or singleflight around check-build-cache would fix it.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same race. Narrowing the cacheMu lock from the whole function to only the final cache assignment lets multiple goroutines build the same index for the same key concurrently.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and counter in concurrent index build loop

In searchSupport.init, every goroutine spawned via group.Go writes to the outer err variable (`_, _, err = s.build(ctx, ...)`) and increments totalBatchesIndexed without any synchronization. With initWorkers > 1 (the whole point of this PR is concurrent namespace builds), these are concurrent reads/writes of shared variables: a Go data race that will fail under -race, the trace event count (span.AddEvent using totalBatchesIndexed) can be wrong, and worse, the closure returns the shared err — if goroutine A's build fails but goroutine B overwrites err with nil before A's `return err` is evaluated, errgroup sees nil and startup succeeds with a failed/missing index. Use a local variable inside the closure (`_, _, berr := s.build(...); return berr`) and an atomic counter (or compute the count from len(stats)).

Watch goroutine panics on closed events channel and uses a never-canceled context

The watch loop started at the end of searchSupport.init uses `watchctx := context.Background()` (so it is never canceled on server shutdown) and then does `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` without checking the receive's ok flag. The SQL backend's poller closes the events channel when the backend stops; receiving from a closed channel returns nil immediately, so handleEvent dereferences a nil *WrittenEvent at `evt.Type` — an unrecovered panic in this goroutine crashes the entire process during shutdown (and absent the panic the loop would spin at 100% CPU). Because this PR makes init run unconditionally at server construction, this goroutine now always starts. It should be `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`, and the context should be tied to the server lifecycle. Note the same unguarded-receive pattern exists in initWatcher in server.go.

No test coverage for the new eager-init contract

NewResourceServer now runs s.Init synchronously and returns an error when backend init or the index build fails, and the s.Init(ctx) guards were removed from every gRPC handler (Create, Update, Delete, Read, List, Watch, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob) — but no test was added or updated to cover the new contract: that construction-time init failures propagate, or that handlers behave correctly without ever calling Init. The only test change in the PR skips the postgres variant of the one integration test that exercises the storage-server target. A unit test around NewResourceServer init success/failure (e.g., with a failing StorageBackend) would catch regressions in this new startup behavior.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() destroys the factory-owned shared queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (also reached via terminate() and join()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory: it is created once in the factory's __init__ and the same instance is passed to every strategy produced by create_with_partitions(). Arroyo's StreamProcessor calls close()+join() on the strategy at every partition revocation/rebalance and then builds a new strategy from the same factory. After the first rebalance the pool's queues have been shut down (queue.Queue.shutdown()) and all worker threads have exited, so every subsequent queue_pool.submit() raises queue.ShutDown from work_queue.put(); that exception is swallowed by SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's except clause, which marks the offset complete so it is committed even though the message was never processed. Net effect: after any routine consumer-group event (deploy, scaling, assignment change) a consumer in thread-queue-parallel mode silently drops all results until the process is restarted. The pool lifecycle should belong only to the factory (strategy.close() should stop just its own commit thread), or the factory should create a fresh pool in create_with_partitions().

submit()'s catch-all marks offsets complete for messages that were never processed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, the broad `except Exception` handler records the message's offset via add_offset + complete_offset, making it committable even though the message was never handed to a worker. Skipping is intentional for undecodable payloads, but those are already handled by decode_payload returning None; this catch-all also fires for real failures — grouping_fn raising, or work_queue.put raising queue.ShutDown once the pool has been shut down (after a rebalance, or during shutdown with in-flight submits). In those cases the offset is committed and the result is silently lost instead of being left uncommitted so it can be re-consumed. Only the intentional skip path (decoder returned None) should complete the offset; unexpected exceptions from grouping/submission should propagate or leave the offset outstanding so the message is retried.

Queues are unbounded, so the advertised 'natural backpressure' does not exist

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, so they are unbounded. The class and strategy docstrings advertise 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but an unbounded queue never fills: if workers fall behind on slow results (the exact problem this PR is meant to mitigate), submit() never blocks and the consumer keeps reading from Kafka and buffering WorkItem objects — each retaining the full original Kafka message — in memory without limit. Under sustained lag this grows memory unboundedly and can OOM the consumer, and it defeats the offset-based flow control since offsets are only committed after processing. Give the queues a maxsize (or otherwise cap in-flight items) so put() blocks and provides real backpressure.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker shutdown flags before draining, so queued items are abandoned

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() first sets worker.shutdown = True for every worker and only then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on `while not self.shutdown`, so a worker that finishes its current item after the flag is set exits its loop immediately, abandoning any items still in its queue — the immediate=False 'drain remaining items' semantics never take effect because no worker is left to read them. Those messages were already fetched from Kafka; their offsets simply never get committed and they will be reprocessed on restart, but the shutdown is not actually graceful as written. Shut the queues down first (immediate=False) so workers drain and then exit via queue.ShutDown, and only use the flag as a backstop.

test_stats_reporting races with workers draining the queue

In test_stats_reporting, the test submits 10 items to a pool whose workers process each item in microseconds, then immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0. Whether anything is still queued at that point is a race between the submitting thread and the three worker threads; on a fast machine the workers can drain all 10 items before get_stats() runs, making this assertion fail intermittently. The test should hold items in the queue with an explicit blocking condition in the processor before asserting non-zero depth, or drop that assertion.

false_positives.candidate:
Set→sorted-set change will WRONGTYPE-fail on segment keys written before the deploy

Segment keys (`span-buf:s:*`) were previously plain Redis sets written with SADD; this PR switches all access to sorted-set commands (ZADD here, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, ZSCAN in _load_segment_data). Existing keys live up to `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), so after a rolling deploy, any batch or flush touching a pre-deploy key raises `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` — the Lua EVALSHA aborts and `p.execute()` raises, failing the whole Kafka batch until those keys expire or are flushed. There is no migration step or type-tolerant handling; this needs an explicit rollout plan (flush the buffer cluster, or drain before enabling).

max_segment_spans is now dead configuration; the only enforcement is a hardcoded 1000 in Lua

The Python-side guard in `_load_segment_data` that skipped segments exceeding `self.max_segment_spans` (and emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) was deleted, but `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001). The only remaining enforcement is the hardcoded `if span_count > 1000` in add-buffer.lua, which neither matches the default (1001) nor any configured value — anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` now gets a silent no-op, and the span-count cap diverges from the documented setting. Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or remove the parameter.

ZUNIONSTORE default AGGREGATE SUM doubles scores of duplicated spans, skewing eviction

`zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` uses Redis's default AGGREGATE SUM, so when the same span payload exists in both source sets (e.g. a duplicate/redelivered span that was previously merged), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps — roughly 2× the real time. Since eviction is `zpopmin` (lowest score first), such a duplicated span is artificially protected from eviction and will survive while genuinely newer spans are dropped. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) so duplicated members keep a sane score.

Redirect-chain limit lowered from 10000 to 1000; over-limit chains silently mis-join segments

The redirect resolution loop now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000. When the limit is hit the loop simply ends with `set_span_id` pointing at a mid-chain span, and the incoming span is merged into that mid-chain set (recreating an unlinked key as a new orphan segment) rather than the segment root — fragmenting the segment into separately flushed pieces. Redirect entries persist for `redis_ttl` (1h) for every span id ever seen, independent of the new 1000-span payload cap, so very active traces can still build chains longer than 1000. If the lower bound is intentional, at least log or metric when the loop exits without resolving (redirect_depth == 1000) so the fragmentation is observable.

end_timestamp_precise is used as a Redis score without validation; one bad span fails the whole batch

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is passed straight through as the ZADD score for the span payload. `rapidjson.loads` accepts NaN/Infinity, and Redis rejects non-finite ZADD scores with an error, so a single malformed span makes the entire `p.execute()` pipeline fail — failing and reprocessing the whole Kafka batch rather than just the bad span. Previously the payload went into a plain set so this value was never interpreted. Sanitize the score (e.g. skip or clamp non-finite values) before building the ZADD mapping.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. The eligibility cache key is built with Python's `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`. Using `hash()` for a cache key is fragile: two different project-id sets in the same organization that collide would share an eligibility decision for 60 seconds, silently applying (or withholding) upsampling for the wrong project set and returning wrong counts. Use an explicit, collision-free key (e.g. the joined sorted ids). Relatedly, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is never called from anywhere in the codebase, so despite its docstring ('should be called when the allowlist configuration changes') nothing invalidates on option changes — and the docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` ('reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time') now contradicts the 60-second caching layered on top of it, which is misleading for the next person touching this code.

The golden comment's specific concern is hash randomization across processes, which breaks key matching between workers and invalidation. The candidate instead raises hash collisions, which is a different failure mode. It does point to the same code and the same fix, so this counts as a partial-to-substantial match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is checked against the request-level dataset/query instead of the scoped dataset/query actually executed

Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over `dataset` and `request` from `get()`, but `_get_event_stats` is invoked with a `scoped_dataset` and a possibly rewritten `query` argument. Similarly, `_is_error_focused_query` reads `request.GET['query']`, so it never sees the augmented `!event.type:transaction` / `event.type:transaction` split queries and can misclassify them. The eligibility check should be based on `scoped_dataset` and the `query` parameter passed into `_get_event_stats`.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental nested git submodule (gitlink) committed

This PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d2909...`, i.e. a gitlink pinning a nested checkout of the sentry repository itself (at this PR's own base commit), with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is almost certainly an accidental artifact of having a local clone inside the working tree. Once merged, every checkout of the repo will contain an uninitializable submodule directory, `git status` will permanently show it, and CI/checkout tooling that recurses or validates submodules may fail. It should be removed from the PR.

upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no NULL fallback, silently dropping unsampled errors

The new `upsampled_count()` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse `sum()` skips NULL values, so any error event whose `sample_weight` is NULL contributes 0 to the count. NULL weights occur for events ingested before the project was allowlisted / before the column existed, and for events the SDK/Relay sent without an `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` context (e.g. projects at sample rate 1.0 that never attach the context). The code comments assert 'sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects', but nothing enforces this: the allowlist is a mutable option applied to projects with pre-existing data. Consequence: for allowlisted projects, `count()` becomes an undercount that silently excludes exactly those events, which is worse than not upsampling at all. The aggregate should coalesce missing weights, e.g. `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, toFloat64(1)))` (or `ifNull(sample_weight, 1)`), so unsampled events count once. Note the new snuba tests only store events that carry the `error_sampling` context, so this failure mode is not covered anywhere.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring matching on the raw query string, producing false positives

`_is_error_focused_query` lowercases `request.GET['query']` and checks `'event.type:error' in query`. This is not a parsed search match: a query like `message:"saw event.type:error in logs"` or a longer value such as `event.type:errortag` contains the substring and will be classified as error-focused. The `count()` → `sum(sample_weight)` transform is then applied to a query that also matches transactions/other events, whose `sample_weight` is NULL, so those events are counted as 0 and the returned counts are wrong. If the intent is to only transform queries that filter to error events, the query should be parsed (or at minimum token-boundary matched) rather than substring-matched.

upsampled_count registered without private=True, exposing an internal-only function in the public query API

The new `SnQLFunction("upsampled_count", ...)` does not set `private=True`, unlike the sibling internal helper directly above it in `function_converter`. Public functions are selectable by any API user in arbitrary discover/events queries (`upsampled_count()` in `field`/`yAxis`) and may surface in docs/function-listing surfaces. Since this function is an implementation detail of the error-upsampling feature (injected by the endpoint itself, which works regardless of visibility) and returns misleading values on non-allowlisted or unsampled data, it should be marked `private=True` to keep it out of the public query surface.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-precedence test caches a non-allowing permission, so it doesn't prove the denial cache wins over cached grants

In the subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry", the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the code stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} in permCache. With a false value the cached permissions would deny the request anyway, so the test would still pass if the denial-cache branch in Check were broken or removed. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name/parent with underscores, which they can themselves contain, allowing key collisions

The key is built as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent with no escaping. Dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so two different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key: e.g. (name="dash_1", parent="x") and (name="dash", parent="1_x") both yield "..._dash_1_x". A denial cached for one resource would then incorrectly deny a different resource/parent combination for up to the 30s TTL. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or otherwise unambiguously encode the fields.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: userPermDenialCacheKey joins its components with underscores, so keys can be ambiguous and collide, which causes incorrect denial cache hits. The candidate adds a concrete collision example and a fix, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is consulted before the permission cache, so a stale denial overrides fresher cached grants

In Check, the denial cache is checked first (lines 116-121) and returns Allowed=false immediately, before the cached permission set is consulted (line 123). Denial entries live for shortCacheTTL (30s) and are never invalidated. Consider: (1) a user is denied resource A after a DB requery, so a denial entry for A is cached; (2) the user is then granted A in the DB; (3) any other cache miss for the same user+action re-queries the DB and refreshes permCache, which now includes A; (4) a new Check for A hits the stale denial entry and returns false even though the server's own fresh permCache would allow it. This reintroduces the exact 'user can't access a resource they were just granted' problem this PR is meant to fix, for up to 30s after any denial. Checking the cached permissions first (allow on positive evidence, then consult the denial cache for the fast-deny path) would avoid contradicting fresher cached grants while keeping the denial fast path.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
OAuth token exchange and user-info fetch can raise unhandled exceptions, producing a 500

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is outside the try/except that only wraps safe_urlread/parse_qsl. A connection error, timeout, or RestrictedIPAddress from sentry.http raises here, and there is no exception handler in the pipeline dispatch path, so a transient GitHub/network failure during installation surfaces as a 500 rather than the graceful error page this PR adds. The same applies to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` on line 434, which performs another network call that can raise. Both calls should be wrapped so failures render the github-integration-failed page as the PR intends.

Ownership check compares mutable GitHub usernames instead of immutable user IDs

The new check compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, i.e. it compares GitHub login names. GitHub usernames are mutable and recyclable: (a) if the user who installed the app later renames their GitHub account, the stored sender login no longer matches and that legitimate user can never link or re-link the installation; (b) conversely, if an attacker registers the abandoned old username, they satisfy this check and can attach the victim's GitHub App installation (installation IDs are sequential and guessable) to their own Sentry organization. test_installation_not_found stubs a 404 for GET /app/installations/{installation_id}, but it submits state "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05", which does not match the pipeline signature used throughout these tests ("9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"). Either drive the flow with the correct state and a bound installation_id so the 404 path is exercised, or rename the test to reflect that it now only tests signature validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) — the literal string "alias" instead of the alias of the provider just created ("idp-alias-" + i in the loop at line 381, and "idp-alias-20" at line 425). false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update compares org-aware (wrapped) original against raw updated model, missing invalidations

In update(), the "original" IdP passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is obtained via getById(...), which wraps the model with createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel when the organization feature is enabled. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to additionally require the linked organization to be enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then evaluates LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() (which includes isEnabled()) on this wrapped original but on the raw updated model, so the two sides are not comparable — and neither matches what defines cache membership, since the cached login lists are filled by idpDelegate.getForLogin(...), which filters on the raw persisted enabled flag. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and are cancelled when the request completes

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163) the legacy write runs in a goroutine whose context is `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10*time.Second, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming apiserver request context. For server requests, the context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which happens immediately after the dual writer returns its response. The 10-second timeout therefore almost never gets to run: every legacy write races with request teardown and will frequently fail with context.Canceled. Since the failure is only recorded in a metric and never logged, mode 3 silently drops the 'safety' legacy writes it exists to perform, leaving legacy and unified storage permanently diverged with no signal. The goroutine context should be derived from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (which preserves values like the logger and user) before applying the timeout.

If unified storage does that, the legacy goroutine and the HTTP handler then concurrently mutate and serialize the same object: the legacy store can overwrite unified's resourceVersion/UID on the object being written to the response — a data race and a potentially corrupted response body. Previously the legacy call was synchronous so mutation ordering was controlled; making it async requires passing `obj.DeepCopyObject()` to the legacy call (same concern applies to the Update path reusing request-scoped objects).

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no ordering guarantees. Two quick successive updates to the same object (or a create immediately followed by an update) can be applied to legacy out of order: the goroutine carrying the newer update may finish before the older one, which then overwrites legacy with stale data. Because legacy errors are only counted in a metric and never logged, nothing surfaces this divergence, and the legacy copy — the stated purpose of mode 3 ('just as a safe measure') — can silently remain at an old revision indefinitely. Legacy writes need per-object serialization (e.g. a single ordered worker/queue) and/or resourceVersion-based conflict handling.

In all four write methods the error from the async legacy call is only passed to `recordLegacyDuration`; the previous implementation logged it (e.g. `log.Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`). For a mode whose purpose is keeping legacy as a safety net, a failing safety net with no log entry makes diagnosis impossible — this would also have made the request-context cancellation bug visible in logs. Mode 3 unit tests never verify that the async legacy write actually happens

The legacy expectations are registered on a testify mock that is shared between the legacy and unified mocks (both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`), and the tests return immediately after the dual-writer call without waiting for the legacy goroutine or calling AssertExpectations. Consequences: (a) the success cases pass even if the legacy call never runs — the request-context cancellation bug in dualwriter_mode3.go fails nothing here; (b) because both backends share one mock, the Create error case registers only a 'legacy' expectation and it is actually `Storage.Create` that matches it, so the test's name and setup do not reflect what is exercised. Use separate mocks and wait/assert on the legacy invocation (e.g. require.Eventually) so each backend's call and ordering is genuinely checked.

`doPlaylistTests` performs k8s writes and then immediately reads through the legacy API (`getFromBothAPIs`, the 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' subtest, and the `/api/playlists` list comparisons) expecting both backends to agree. Under mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these cross-backend assertions race the legacy goroutine — they pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling (and fail outright whenever the legacy write is cancelled at request end, per the context bug in dualwriter_mode3.go). The two new mode-3 runs of this shared test need to poll for convergence on the legacy side (e.g. require.Eventually) or use relaxed expectations.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded during web requests, so fallbacks silently fail in mailers, background jobs, and other non-request code

Translations are loaded lazily per-locale by the translate accelerator: I18n.translate only loads config.locale, and the only place that loads the full fallback chain (current locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en) is this new before_filter via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Any code that translates outside the request cycle (Sidekiq jobs, ActionMailer views, rake tasks, console, plugins) never runs set_locale, so in those processes only the active locale's yml file is ever loaded. When a key is missing in that locale, I18n::Backend::Fallbacks will dutifully try the site default and :en, but those locales' translations were never loaded into the backend, so the lookup raises MissingTranslationData and the output is a 'translation missing: ...' string instead of the English/default fallback this PR is meant to provide. The loading of the fallback chain should live in the accelerator itself (e.g., in I18n.translate/load_locale, iterate I18n.fallbacks[config.locale] and ensure each locale is loaded) rather than only in ApplicationController#set_locale.

No tests cover the new server-side fallback behavior

This PR changes translation lookup for every locale in every environment (fallback chain current locale -> SiteSetting.default_locale -> :en, lazy loading of that chain via FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!, and removal of config.i18n.fallbacks from the environment configs), but adds no specs. Nothing verifies that a key missing from the active locale falls back to the site default and then to :en, that FallbackLocaleList#[] builds the expected chain (including uniq/compact behavior when locale == default == :en), or that ensure_loaded! actually loads every locale in the chain. A regression here would surface as untranslated or 'translation missing' strings across the whole site, so coverage of this initializer and the set_locale integration is warranted before merging.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

traceID field silently dropped from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line

That code is removed, and the log line now relies entirely on m.logger.FromContext(ctx), which only picks up the contextual attributes injected by the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext: endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy host values are inserted raw and may silently stop matching after migration

The migration copies values from the legacy `embeddable_hosts` setting straight into the new table with `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, ...) VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`. The old `SiteSetting.allows_embeddable_host?` stripped `http(s)://` prefixes when matching (and the old specs explicitly covered scheme-prefixed entries working), but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares the bare hostname (`uri.host`) against the stored value with `lower(host) = ?`. The model strips schemes/paths in `before_validation`, but the migration bypasses the model, so any legacy entries stored as `http://example.com`, with paths, uppercase, or trailing `\r` from Windows line endings will be inserted verbatim and will never match again — embedding silently breaks for those sites. Additionally the value is interpolated directly into the SQL string, so a host containing a single quote produces invalid SQL and fails the migration; values should be normalized and passed through quoting/bound parameters.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the embed_category site setting row is missing or unmatched

The migration computes the default category with `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. site_settings only contains rows for settings an admin explicitly changed, and `embed_category` defaulted to blank, so for the vast majority of installations (and every fresh install) this query returns zero rows. Indexing `[0]` on an empty result set returns nil (or raises IndexError depending on the pg adapter version), so `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError and the entire migration aborts, blocking the upgrade. The fallback for `category_id == 0` on line 15 (`... WHERE name = 'uncategorized_category_id'")[0]['value']`) has the same problem if that row is absent. Both lookups need to tolerate an empty result (e.g. `.first` with a nil check or a begin/rescue) before dereferencing.

false_positives.candidate:
Host validation accepts ports but record lookup can never match them

The validation regex `/\A[a-z0-9]+([\-\.]{1}[a-z0-9]+)*\.[a-z]{2,5}(:[0-9]{1,5})?(\/.*)?\Z/i` explicitly permits an optional `:port` suffix, so an admin can successfully save `example.com:3000`. However `record_for_host` compares `uri.host` — which never includes the port — against the stored value, so a host saved with a port will never match and embedding from it will always be rejected. Either strip the port in `before_validation` like the scheme/path are stripped, or disallow it in the regex.

Host regex rejects valid TLDs longer than 5 characters

The TLD portion of the validation regex is `[a-z]{2,5}`, which rejects real domains under longer TLDs such as `.museum`, `.travel`, or `.technology`. The previous free-form site setting accepted these hosts, so sites embedding from such domains can no longer add them through the new admin UI. The TLD segment should allow a more generous length (e.g. `{2,}`).

New host saved without choosing a category shows a blank category until reload

In the `save` action, after the record is created the component runs `host.set('category', Discourse.Category.findById(this.get('categoryId')))`. For a newly added host the `categoryId` property starts as null (the user is not required to pick a category; the server substitutes `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id`), so `findById(null)` returns undefined and the row's category badge renders blank even though the server assigned the uncategorized category. The correct category only appears after a full page reload. The component should resolve the category from the category_id returned in the save response when `categoryId` is unset.

New admin controllers have no request-level specs

Both new controller specs (`admin/embeddable_hosts_controller_spec.rb` and `admin/embedding_controller_spec.rb`) only assert that the controller is a subclass of Admin::AdminController. There is no coverage for create/update/destroy behavior, validation errors, the category defaulting to uncategorized, or the unknown-id case — which is how the nil-host NoMethodError in `update`/`destroy` slips through. At minimum, request specs exercising the happy paths and the missing-record paths should be added.

totalPages off-by-one when member count is a multiple of the page size

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit this overcounts by one page (e.g. 100 members at limit 50 gives 3 pages instead of 2; 50 members gives 2 instead of 1). Because the next action is enabled until currentPage == totalPages, the admin can page to offset == user_count, and the server then returns an empty member list, rendering a phantom empty last page. This should be Math.ceil(user_count / limit).

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members page is silently truncated to 50 members

Previously #members returned the full member list for non-automatic groups (only automatic groups were limited, default 200). It now always paginates with a default limit of 50. The public-facing group members page (group-members route and group/members.hbs) calls findMembers() once and has no pagination controls — pagination UI was only added to the admin template — so any group with more than 50 members now shows only the first 50 on its public members page, with no way to view the rest.

remove_member raises RecordNotFound when the user is not a member

remove_member calls group.users.delete(user_id) with an Integer id. Rails resolves numeric arguments via find on the association, which raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound if that user is not in the group, producing a 404/500 instead of a successful no-op. This is easy to hit in practice (e.g. two admins removing the same user, or a retry after the member list was reloaded). Use a lookup that tolerates absence, e.g. delete the join record scoped by user_id, or find_by(id:) and skip when nil.

{{#unless automatic}} always true inside the item view, so remove link shows for automatic groups

This template is rendered by the group-member item view whose context is the member (a User), which has no `automatic` property, so {{#unless automatic}} always evaluates true and the remove (×) link is rendered even for members of automatic groups. Clicking it fires removeMember, which the server rejects with 422 can_not_modify_automatic, and the client-side removeMember promise has no rejection handler, so the admin gets no feedback at all. The automatic flag needs to come from the group/controller (e.g. passed into the item view) rather than being looked up on the member.

add_members does not strip whitespace around usernames and fails silently

add_members splits the usernames param on ',' but never strips the pieces, so input like "alice, bob" looks up the literal username " bob", finds nothing, and silently skips it — the action still returns success_json. An admin adding multiple users can get a success response while some users were never added. Strip each username (and/or report which names were not found) before the find_by_username call.

No spec coverage for the changed /groups/:group_id/members response contract

This PR changes GET /groups/:group_id/members from a bare serialized array to an object shaped {members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}} and introduces default pagination, but the spec changes only cover Admin::GroupsController — there is no request/controller spec asserting the new response shape, the meta values, or the default limit/offset behavior. Any pre-existing spec for #members would also now fail against the new shape. Add coverage for the new contract.

Validator performs DB writes during validation; match_count is double-counted per signup

validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which as a side effect increments match_count and sets last_match_at on the blocked_emails row. Validation is normally read-only, and here it runs more than once per signup: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` at line 168 (before the DiscourseHub check) and then `user.save` at line 172, which validates again — so one blocked signup attempt records two matches. Blocking `spammer@example.com` therefore does nothing to stop `Spammer@example.com` or `SPAMMER@example.com` from registering — the lookup misses the row and a separate account is created. The block should normalize case (store emails lowercase and compare against `email.downcase`) to be effective as an anti-abuse control.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same problem: the email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? is case-sensitive, so a block can be bypassed by changing the letter case of the email.

In BlockedEmail.should_block?, `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both read the same value, so one increment is silently lost. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")` or `update_counters`, which also avoids re-running validations and callbacks for a stats update.

rejectedEmails array is defined on the prototype and shared across instances

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` in the hash passed to `Discourse.Controller.extend` puts a single mutable array on the controller's prototype, shared by every instance. The app currently instantiates this controller once, but any second instantiation — in JS tests, or if the controller is torn down and recreated — inherits emails rejected during earlier usage, and mutations via `pushObject` leak between instances. true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`-ms-align-items` is not a real property

The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`, but no Microsoft flexbox implementation ever supported that property — IE10's 2012 'tweener' syntax uses `-ms-flex-align` (which the mixin already emits on the previous line). true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say -ms-align-items is not a real property and that -ms-flex-align is the correct legacy IE property. The candidate adds that the mixin already emits -ms-flex-align, but the core issue is the same.

Previously that button was pinned to the right edge of the post row; now it will be packed immediately after `.small-action-desc` on the left, because the container has no `justify-content: space-between` and the button has no `margin-left: auto`. If the button is a direct child (as the old float-based layout implies), this is a visible layout regression for small action posts (e.g. undo/expand controls). Either add `-moz-box-align: $alignment;` to the mixin or drop the `-moz-box` display fallbacks so the mixin set is self-consistent.

Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. It is therefore never invoked, and `website_name` is always serialized — including `"website_name": null` for users who have no website set. Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same main issue as the golden comment: include_website_name is missing its '?' suffix, so the conditional inclusion never applies. It does not mention the secondary string-mutation concern, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:

This serializer deliberately hides `website` (along with bio/location/etc.) for trust-level-0 users viewed by logged-out visitors, via `untrusted_attributes`, which defines `include_website?` to return false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. Fix by adding `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` (or honoring `scope.restrict_user_fields?` in its include check) and add a spec covering an anonymous view of a TL0 user with a website.

The `elsif` branch drops the first dot-separated label of both the website host and the instance host and compares the remainders whenever both hosts have the same number of labels (> 2). That works for the intended `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com` case, but it also matches completely unrelated sites that share a parent or public suffix: e.g. website `example.co.uk` with instance `another.co.uk` compares `co.uk == co.uk`, and `alice.github.io` vs `bob.github.io` compares `github.io == github.io`, causing the profile to display the full URL path of an unrelated website. website_name is stale after the user edits their website

Previously the displayed label was a computed property (`websiteName`) derived from `model.website`, so editing the website in preferences updated the profile display immediately. Now the label comes from the server as `website_name`, and the `save()` success handler only applies `bio_excerpt` from the PUT response, discarding the recomputed `website_name` even though the server returns it. After changing their website, the user keeps seeing the old label on their profile until a full page reload. Apply `data.user.website_name` (and ideally `website`) from the save response, or refetch the user.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage targetOrigin is the full referer URL — browsers throw and the iframe never resizes

The layout calls parent.postMessage({type: 'discourse-resize', height: ...}, '<%= request.referer %>'). The referer is a full URL with a path (e.g. http://blog.example.com/2013/02/post.html), but targetOrigin must be an origin (scheme://host[:port]); Chrome/Firefox throw a SyntaxError ('Invalid target origin') for anything else. As a result the discourse-resize message is never delivered to the parent page and the embed.js auto-resize feature simply never works. The code should post to the referer's origin only. Additionally, the referer is interpolated into a single-quoted JS string and html_escape does not escape apostrophes on all Rails versions this repo supports, so a referer containing a raw ' would also break the script.

false_positives.candidate:
RSS feed content is stored as raw, unsanitized HTML — stored XSS on the forum domain

PollFeed takes each feed item's HTML (CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)) and passes it to TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html] (app/models/topic_embed.rb:22). Post#cook returns `raw` unchanged for raw_html posts (app/models/post.rb:133), so `cooked` contains the feed markup verbatim with zero sanitization, and it is rendered unescaped (<%= raw post.cooked %> in app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19, and as cooked HTML in the main app). Any <script> or on* handler in a feed item becomes stored XSS executing on the forum domain for every visitor. The CGI.unescapeHTML makes this worse: the XML parser already decodes entities once, so content the feed author properly escaped (e.g. `<script>` in a code sample) is decoded a second time into live markup — even a fully trusted blog can inject live scripts. Note the import_remote path at least whitelists tags/attributes via Readability; the RSS path sanitizes nothing. Feed content should be run through Sanitize (or an equivalent whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

Server-side fetch follows redirects to any host — SSRF past the embeddable_host check

TopicRetriever#invalid_host? only validates that URI(embed_url).host == SiteSetting.embeddable_host, but TopicEmbed.import_remote fetches with `open(url)` (open-uri), which transparently follows HTTP redirects to arbitrary hosts. An open redirect on the allowed host (e.g. http://blog.example.com/out?u=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data or an intranet address) lets an external requester make the forum server fetch internal URLs; the response is then Readability-parsed and published as a public topic, exfiltrating the content. The fetch layer should validate every redirect target against the allowed host or disable cross-host redirects.

Loading page self-reload fails the controller's referer check — embed gets stuck on 403

The loading page reloads itself every 30s via document.location.reload() so it picks up the topic once the RetrieveTopic job finishes. A programmatic reload sends the iframe's own URL (the /embed/best URL on the forum host) as the Referer, not the embedding page's URL. EmbedController#ensure_embeddable (app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:26) compares URI(referer).host to SiteSetting.embeddable_host and raises Discourse::InvalidAccess on mismatch, so the reload gets a 403 and the embed is permanently stuck on an error page instead of showing the newly imported topic. The referer check needs to also accept the forum's own embed URL (or the loading flow needs another mechanism, e.g. message-bus).

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs (//host/path)

The relative-URL rewrite treats any href/src starting with '/' as host-relative: a protocol-relative URL like //cdn.example.com/a.png matches `href.start_with?('/')` and is rewritten to http://blog.example.com/cdn.example.com/a.png, producing a broken link. Protocol-relative URLs are common in feed/article HTML. The check should exclude values starting with '//' (and ideally also absolutize paths that don't start with '/', which are currently left relative and break in the forum context).

URIs that pass the regex but are invalid crash the whole import run

URLs are only validated against /^https?:\/\// before URI(url) is called in absolutize_urls (and open(url) in import_remote). Feed links or embed URLs containing spaces or other characters illegal in URIs (e.g. 'http://example.com/my post.html') pass the regex but raise URI::InvalidURIError here, which is not rescued — in PollFeed this aborts the entire hourly run so no further feed items are imported, and in the RetrieveTopic job it causes repeated sidekiq retries. Validate with URI.parse in a begin/rescue and skip bad items instead of aborting.

ADD COLUMN with DEFAULT + NOT NULL rewrites the entire posts table and blocks writes

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false forces PostgreSQL (< 11) to rewrite every row of the posts table while holding an AccessExclusiveLock. posts is the largest table in a Discourse install, so on any sizable forum this migration blocks all posting/reading for minutes during a deploy. Safer pattern: add the column without a default, backfill in batches, then set the default and the NOT NULL constraint.

Find-then-create race on embed_url unique index aborts concurrent import jobs

import does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and later TopicEmbed.create! inside a transaction. Two concurrent jobs for the same URL (a RetrieveTopic job racing the hourly PollFeed, or two RetrieveTopic jobs for staff, who bypass the redis throttle) both see no existing embed and both build a topic and post; the second create! hits the unique index on topic_embeds.embed_url and raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, failing that job — and in PollFeed, aborting the rest of the feed items. Rescue RecordNotUnique/re-check inside the transaction or use an upsert-style create_or_find.

Non-atomic setnx + expire can permanently throttle an embed URL

retrieved_recently? does $redis.setnx(retrieved_key, '1') followed by a separate $redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60). If the process crashes (or expire raises) between the two calls, the key never expires and retrieve() will treat that embed_url as recently retrieved forever — the topic is never fetched. Use a single atomic SET with an EX option (supported by redis-rb) instead of the two-step dance.

This changes the shipped 20131223171005_create_top_topics migration to create_table :top_topics, force: true. Databases that already ran the migration will never re-run it, so the change is a silent no-op there; on fresh or restored setups, force: true will silently DROP and recreate the table (and any data) if it already exists. Released migrations shouldn't be modified — add a new migration instead. The new db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb uses force: true too, carrying the same silent-drop risk.

The tests 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' never enable the preceding conditions: feed_polling_enabled? defaults to false in the test env (and the URL is unset in the username test), so execute short-circuits at the first condition and `poller.expects(:poll_feed).never` passes regardless of the condition under test. These specs would still pass if the url/username presence checks were removed entirely. Each gating test should stub all the prior conditions to true so only the condition under test fails.

The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
