The candidate does not explicitly mention the 413 handler, but it covers the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Downsize loop reads size from a stale file handle and ignores downsize failures

The loop condition `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` uses Tempfile#size, which is fstat() on the already-open file handle. OptimizedImage.downsize -> convert_with runs ImageOptim.optimize_image!, which — when it improves the image (the common case) — replaces the file at tempfile.path by moving a newly written file over it, i.e. a new inode. The open handle keeps pointing at the old, unlinked inode, so tempfile.size stays frozen at the size captured after the first convert and never reflects further reductions. Consequences: (1) an image that needs more than one pass to get under the limit is downsized all 5 times — shrunk to 0.8^5 ≈ 33% of its dimensions and lossily recompressed/optimized five times, degrading quality and burning CPU; (2) the same stale tempfile.size is passed to Upload.create_for on line 72, so an image that was actually reduced below the limit can be stored with, and validated against, its old larger filesize and still be rejected. The loop also ignores OptimizedImage.downsize's return value, so a failing convert is retried identically five times. Check File.size(tempfile.path), pass that value to create_for, and break out of the loop when downsize returns false.

With two override windows on the same date (e.g. 10:00-11:00 and 14:00-15:00), a slot at 14:30 is rejected because it is outside the first window, and a slot at 10:30 is rejected because it is outside the second window. Only a single override window per date works correctly. The check needs 'there exists an override on this date that contains the slot' semantics rather than short-circuiting on the first non-containing override.

Override containment check treats partial overlap as available and misses the exact end boundary

The conditions used to decide that a slot is outside an override are `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` and `slotStartTime > overrideEnd` (strict isAfter). Anything else — including a slot that starts before the override and ends inside it, or starts inside and ends after it — is treated as 'within the override' and the host is considered available, even though part of the slot falls outside the override window. Additionally, a slot starting exactly at the override end fails the strict `isAfter` and is also treated as inside the override. For round-robin events where slots are generated from other hosts' working hours, this lets fixed hosts be booked outside their override window. `dayjs(date.start)` creates a dayjs in the server machine's local timezone, and `.add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` is compared against `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`, where slotStartTime is in UTC mode. prisma is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService

This is a `Cannot find name 'prisma'` type-check failure / ReferenceError at runtime, so the build breaks and the Salesforce integration cannot work at all.

Sync-path Response object is persisted as the HubSpot credential key, destroying the stored credential

`refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when credential sync is enabled, but the result is typed/used as `HubspotToken`. In the sync path: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined so `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` sets undefined, and `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes a Response object — i.e. the stored credential key is overwritten with `{"expiryDate": null}`. `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the self-hoster's sync endpoint, but Zoom's app slug everywhere else is "zoom" (see zoomvideo/api/callback.ts which stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new webhook endpoint which looks up `prisma.app` by slug). The platform cannot resolve "zoomvideo" to the Zoom app, so token refresh via the sync endpoint will fail for Zoom. Every other app passes its real slug ("google-calendar", "msteams", "webex", etc.).

axios response shape assumed, but sync path returns a fetch Response

The normal refresh function returns an AxiosResponse (read via `tokenInfo.data`), but `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when sync is enabled, which has no `.data`. `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, so Zoho Bigin token refresh always crashes when credential sync is enabled. The same class of mismatch applies to zohocrm.

axios/fetch response mismatch breaks ZohoCRM refresh when sync is enabled

The wrapped refresh function returns an AxiosResponse, but the sync branch of `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` with no `.data` property. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` therefore throws a TypeError; it is swallowed by `catch (e) { this.log.error(e); }`, leaving `this.accessToken` unset/stale. All subsequent Zoho CRM API calls go out with an empty or expired `Zoho-oauthtoken` header and fail, silently breaking the integration for synced users.

Webex refresh always rejects when credential sync is enabled

Unlike the other apps, webex kept validating with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`, and literal `scope`/`token_type` values. The documented sync-endpoint contract ("response should only contain the access token and expiry date") can never satisfy this schema, so `parsedToken.success` is always false and refresh always rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — Webex is broken whenever credential sync is on.

Lark refresh expects Lark's {code, data} envelope but sync endpoint returns a flat minimal payload

The sync-path response from `refreshOAuthTokens` is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>` and then read as `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, etc. The sync endpoint returns a flat `{access_token, expiry}` payload (per the documented contract in refreshOAuthTokens), so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws (or stores undefined token fields into the credential key). findFirst by userId+appId can overwrite the wrong credential for multi-account apps

Cal.com allows a user to connect multiple accounts for the same app (e.g. several Google or Office 365 calendars), producing multiple Credential rows with the same userId and appId. The webhook's `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key with the pushed credentials, so the platform can silently clobber the tokens of a different account than intended. The payload needs an account identifier (e.g. email/external id) to target the correct credential.

Outbound request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication

The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no shared secret, signature, or header (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is only checked on the inbound webhook). The platform endpoint therefore cannot verify the request genuinely comes from its Cal.com instance; anyone who can reach that endpoint can request freshly refreshed third-party OAuth tokens for any user id / app. The implementation should include the shared secret (or an HMAC) so the platform can authenticate the caller.

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This change adds a new authenticated credential-writing endpoint and rewires token refresh for nine integrations with two divergent code paths (direct provider refresh vs. platform sync endpoint); the response-shape mismatches introduced here (axios vs fetch, GaxiosResponse vs fetch Response) are exactly the kind of regression a small unit/integration test per service would have caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. The previous version of this function collected the reminder deletions and awaited them via Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)); now nothing reminder-related is awaited. On a serverless platform the invocation can be frozen once the response is sent, before these floating promises finish — the cancelled flag is then never persisted, the cron never cancels the SendGrid scheduled send, and the reminder email is still delivered, i.e. the exact bug this PR fixes persists intermittently. Collect the promises and await them before returning.

It only covers the booking-cancel location rather than every location the golden comment lists, but the underlying bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

immediateDelete path neither deletes nor flags the reminder row and has no retry on failure

When immediateDelete is true (used by the reschedule flow in handleNewBooking and by workflow/step deletion in the workflows router), deleteScheduledEmailReminder only posts the cancel to SendGrid and returns — it never deletes the WorkflowReminder row and never sets cancelled=true. Two consequences: (1) if the SendGrid request fails, the catch only logs and nothing retries — the row keeps scheduled=true and cancelled=null, so the old booking's reminder email is still sent (duplicates after a reschedule); (2) in the reschedule flow the stale rows (scheduled=true, referenceId set, cancelled=null) linger in the DB until the cron's past-date deleteMany removes them days later, unlike every other cancellation path which deletes or flags the row. Consider deleting the row (or marking it cancelled as a fallback) even in the immediate path, so a failed SendGrid call is retried by the cron instead of being silently lost.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that the immediateDelete=true path cancels the SendGrid email but never deletes or flags the WorkflowReminder row. Both note this leaves orphaned records and is inconsistent with the other cancellation paths. The candidate does not mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE API call, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the entire cancellation batch for the cron run

The new cancellation block wraps the whole for-loop in a single try/catch. If client.request throws for any one reminder (transient SendGrid error, invalid/already-cancelled batch_id, or SendGrid rejecting a cancel that is too close to the scheduled send time), execution jumps straight to the catch: (a) every remaining reminder in remindersToCancel is skipped for that run, and (b) none of the prisma.workflowReminder.delete calls collected so far actually execute, because they are only awaited after the loop via Promise.all and Prisma promises are lazy (they don't run until awaited). On the next cron run the same rows are re-fetched (still cancelled=true) and the loop aborts again at the same poisoned row, so a single bad reminder can block cancellation of all pending cancelled reminders until its own scheduledDate passes — at which point the first deleteMany in this handler silently drops the row and the email has already been sent. Each loop iteration needs its own try/catch (and each row should be deleted right after its own successful cancel) so one failure doesn't stall the queue.

Deferred-only cancellation still misses reminders cancelled close to their send time

With this PR, cancellation of scheduled emails happens exclusively in this cron job, which runs every 15 minutes and only cancels reminders whose scheduledDate is within the next hour. If a booking is cancelled shortly before a reminder's send time, the next cron run may not happen before SendGrid sends the email, and SendGrid does not allow changing the status of a scheduled send that is about to go out — so the reminder is delivered for a cancelled booking even though the cancellation was recorded in time. Consider using the immediate path (deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true, already used in the reschedule flow) for reminders whose scheduledDate is near (e.g. within the next hour), and deferring only far-future cancellations to the cron. That still avoids the 100-pending-cancellations limit while closing the last-minute gap.

Newly added reschedule reminder-cancellation is fire-and-forget

In the reschedule flow, the loop that cancels the original booking's workflow reminders calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) and deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...) without awaiting them, and the surrounding try/catch cannot observe their completion (the functions also swallow their own errors). If the serverless invocation is frozen after the response is sent before these promises finish, the original booking's SendGrid batches are never cancelled while the new booking's reminders are scheduled — so both old and new reminders fire, the duplicate-reminder bug for rescheduled bookings this PR is meant to fix. Await these calls.

This handler previously awaited the reminder cleanup via `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`; the refactor removed that and now calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder without await inside forEach. The cancelled flag / row deletion these calls perform is the only thing preventing reminders for the cancelled booking from being sent, so for reliability they should be collected and awaited rather than left floating in a serverless handler.

WorkflowReminder row is leaked when Twilio cancel fails

In deleteScheduledSMSReminder, if twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId) throws (transient error, or the message was already sent), the catch skips the prisma.workflowReminder.delete call. The row is then left behind with scheduled=true and cancelled unset, and — unlike the email path, which flags rows for the cron to retry — nothing ever retries SMS cancellation, so the row leaks permanently and, for transient Twilio failures, the SMS is still delivered for a cancelled booking. Previously the callers deleted these rows in an awaited Promise.all regardless of the Twilio result. Delete the row even when the Twilio cancel fails (or add a retry path).

Prisma import is no longer used

The refactor removed all remaining uses of the Prisma namespace in this file (the deleted code was the last place referencing Prisma.BatchPayload), but the import was kept and even changed from `import type` to a value import. `Prisma` is now an unused import in this module (PrismaPromise is still used), which the repo's lint rules (no-unused-vars) will flag.

No tests for the reworked reminder-cancellation pipeline

This is the second attempt to fix reminders being sent for cancelled/rescheduled bookings — the first fix silently failed in production for an extended period — yet the PR adds no tests covering the new mechanism: setting cancelled=true on cancel/reschedule, the cron cancellation loop (including its all-or-nothing failure behavior when a SendGrid request fails), and the reschedule cancellation in handleNewBooking. Regression coverage around handleCancelBooking and scheduleEmailReminders would materially reduce the risk of another silent failure of this fix.

The blacklist entries are lowercased but the incoming guest string is not, so `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entirely. true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team permission check uses && instead of ||, rejecting team admins

The authorization check computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. isTeamAdmin already matches memberships with role ADMIN or OWNER, so AND-ing it with isTeamOwner makes the whole expression equivalent to "user is team owner". Team admins — whom the variable name and the feature intend to allow — will always fail this check and hit the FORBIDDEN branch, so they cannot add guests to team bookings. The `&&` should be `||`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the team admin/owner permission check uses && where it should use ||. The candidate adds detail about the consequence, which is that team admins get rejected.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type settings that disable standard emails

Every other send* function in this file accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails when eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail is set (event types can disable standard emails, e.g. for custom workflows/platform customers). sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata parameter and addGuests.handler doesn't pass one, so organizers and attendees of event types with standard emails disabled will still receive "Guests Added" and booking-confirmation emails whenever a guest is added, breaking that contract. Thread eventTypeMetadata through and honor the disable flags.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say sendAddGuestsEmails doesn't honor the event type metadata flags that disable standard emails, so hosts and attendees still get emailed. The candidate describes the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add guests, triggering organizer-branded emails to arbitrary addresses

The handler authorizes the request when `isAttendee` is true — any person whose email happens to be on the booking can call viewer.bookings.addGuests with arbitrary addresses. Each call sends an AttendeeScheduledEmail "from" the organizer (replyTo the organizer) to the new addresses plus a notification to every existing attendee. A malicious attendee can therefore spam third parties using the organizer's identity and the booking's legitimacy, with no consent from the organizer and no cap on guests per call. If attendee-initiated guest additions are intentional, this needs rate limiting and sending from the attendee's identity; otherwise the endpoint should be restricted to the organizer and team admins/owners.

Calendar update uses the requester's credentials, not the organizer's, after attendees are already written

`eventManager` is built from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person making the request — but the calendar event being updated lives on the organizer's calendar (booking.user, which is already fetched with credentials in the booking query but never used). When a team owner/admin or an attendee adds guests, EventManager.updateCalendarAttendees searches the requester's credentials for one matching booking.references, which is either missing (throws) or belongs to the wrong user. Because prisma.booking.update has already created the Attendee rows before this call and the call is not wrapped in error handling, the mutation then returns an error even though the guests were persisted: the user sees "unable to add guests", the organizer's calendar event is never updated with the new attendees, and retrying fails with "emails_must_be_unique_valid" because the attendees already exist. Use the organizer's credentials and make the flow failure-safe (e.g., update the calendar before committing, or handle errors so the user is not told the operation failed when it half-succeeded).

No check on booking status or date before adding guests

After loading the booking, the handler never checks booking.status or the booking time, so guests can be added to CANCELLED, REJECTED, PENDING or past bookings. This is reachable from the UI for past confirmed bookings (BookingListItem renders the Edit → "Additional guests" action for `isBookingInPast && isConfirmed`) and via direct API calls for cancelled/rejected ones. Adding a guest to a cancelled booking emails them an AttendeeScheduledEmail with a CONFIRMED ics for an event that no longer exists and permanently attaches attendees to a dead booking. Reject non-ACCEPTED and past bookings before creating attendees.

Adding guests to seated events bypasses seat reservation logic

For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be created together with a BookingSeat record (the handleSeats flow) so that seat availability is counted and the attendee can later cancel/reschedule their seat. This handler blindly creates plain Attendee rows via createMany for any event type, so for seated events the new guests consume no seat — the slot can be overbooked through the normal booking flow afterwards — and the guests have no seat reference for seat-based operations. The handler should either reject seated event types or route through the seat-booking logic.

New guests are stored with the organizer's timeZone and locale

guestsFullDetails sets `timeZone: organizer.timeZone` and `locale: organizer.locale` for every added guest. The AttendeeScheduledEmail sent to those guests renders the meeting time in the attendee's stored timezone — which is actually the organizer's — so guests in other timezones see a wrong local time presented as theirs, and the attendee record permanently carries the wrong timezone/locale (affecting reminders and future emails too). Consider storing a neutral value or making clear whose timezone is displayed.

No limit on number of guests per request

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no .max(), and each call sends an email to every existing attendee plus every new guest, and performs a calendar update. A single request can add hundreds of guests, fanning out hundreds of emails and a large calendar payload — an abuse and performance footgun even for a legitimate organizer. Add a sane .max() on the array and consider a per-booking total guest limit.

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The PR adds a new authenticated mutation that performs a non-trivial permission matrix (organizer vs team admin vs team owner vs attendee vs stranger), dedupes against existing attendees and a blacklist, writes Attendee rows, updates calendars and sends emails, but adds no unit or integration tests. The permission matrix, duplicate/blacklist filtering, seated-event handling and cancelled-booking behavior are exactly where this implementation has defects; tests covering those cases should be added before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code redemption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The login flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then writes the updated array back in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent sign-in requests presenting the same backup code can both decrypt and pass `indexOf` before either update commits, so a code intended to be single-use can be redeemed twice. Use a transaction with a conditional update (or a per-code consumed flag updated atomically) so only one request can consume a given code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same race condition. Backup codes are decrypted, checked, and written back non-atomically, so concurrent logins can redeem the same single-use code twice.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login can skip password verification entirely

In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password check at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the new backup-code branch at line 131 verifies only the backup code. A crafted request to the credentials callback containing a valid `backupCode` together with any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips `verifyPassword` and is authenticated solely by the backup code — a static, 40-bit secret that users store in files/notes. Backup codes are meant to substitute for the authenticator as the second factor, not to replace the password, so a leaked backup code alone yields full account access. The password should be verified (when the user has one) before accepting a backup code, or the flow branching should be keyed off the presence of `backupCode` instead of piggybacking on the `totpCode` gate.

missing_backup_codes message directs users to a settings option that does not exist

The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes outside the initial 2FA setup. Every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped has `backupCodes = null`; if they lose their authenticator and use the new "Lost access" link at login, they hit `MissingBackupCodes` and are told to do something impossible — they cannot log in to reach settings, and even in settings there is no regeneration option. These users are effectively locked out (admin intervention required). Either add a regeneration flow or change the message.

No test exercises the actual backup-code authentication behavior

The only test additions assert that the download/copy/close buttons render on the post-enable screen. Nothing tests the security-critical behavior of the feature: logging in with a backup code, that a redeemed code is invalidated and cannot be reused, that the password is still required alongside a backup code (see the related finding on password skipping), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The added TODO comment ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the unchecked PR checklist item concede this. For an authentication feature, the login-with-backup-code and single-use-invalidation paths should be covered before merge.

Consumed backup codes are nulled instead of removed

After a successful redemption the code does `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts the array, so the stored value permanently accumulates null placeholders (e.g. `[null, null, "abc123...", ...]`). Single-use still works because `indexOf` no longer matches the redeemed string, but the stored blob grows with junk entries and reveals exactly how many codes have been used. Splice the element out (or filter nulls) before re-encrypting.

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashing

Backup codes are stored via `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`. Unlike the TOTP secret, the stored codes are never read back for display — the one-time display uses the in-memory values returned by this same endpoint, and login/disable only need an equality check — so they could be stored as one-way hashes (like passwords). As implemented, anyone who obtains both the database and the encryption key recovers every user's unused backup codes in cleartext.

Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step loses the codes with no recovery path

The backup codes are shown exactly once on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step, and only the explicit Close button calls `onEnable()`. If the user dismisses the dialog at this step in any other way (ESC key or the dialog's close control, which fire `onOpenChange`), the modal closes without `onEnable` being called and the codes — which exist only in this component's React state — can never be displayed or regenerated again. The user's only recourse is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Consider intercepting dismissal on this step with a warning, or providing a way to regenerate codes later.

Copy button shows a success toast even when the clipboard write fails

The copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without awaiting or catching it, then immediately fires `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")`. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied, `writeText` rejects (an unhandled promise rejection) while the user is told the codes were copied — they may close the dialog believing they have codes they don't. Await the promise and only show the success toast on fulfillment, with an error toast on rejection.

Backup codes unusable in the SAML/Google TOTP login flow

When a user with 2FA logs in via Google/SAML they are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` (`totpEmail` set), and in that state the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only offers Cancel — there is no "Lost access" option, so these users cannot enter a backup code even though the credentials provider would accept one. Accounts that enabled 2FA and later moved to an identity-provider login (e.g. after linking Google, which nulls the password) have no self-service recovery path if they lose their authenticator.

Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from keyboard navigation in every `PasswordField` across the app, while it keeps only an sr-only label. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reach the control to verify what they typed. If the goal was to streamline tab order, this trades away an accessibility affordance; consider leaving it focusable.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and turns deletion failures into unhandled rejections

The callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` was changed to `async` so it can `await getCalendar(...)`, but `forEach` does not collect or return the promises produced by an async callback. The `try { ... } catch` block wrapping the loop (lines 124–139) can therefore no longer catch anything: any synchronous throw that the catch previously handled (e.g. a CalendarService constructor error from `new CalendarService(credential)` inside `getCalendar`) and any rejection from the dynamic import, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` now escapes as an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes Node ≥15 server processes by default and never reaches the `logger.error` path. Additionally, because the callback suspends at the first `await getCalendar(...)`, the `deleteEvent` calls are not even initiated before the function moves on to send the reschedule email and return `true`; in a serverless environment the function can finish (and be frozen) before the calendar/video deletions ever run, leaving stale events on users' calendars while the booking is already marked CANCELLED. Fix by replacing the forEach with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say failures from awaiting getCalendar (the dynamic import) are not handled. The golden comment suggests adding a try-catch around the await. The candidate explains that the existing try/catch can't catch these failures because the forEach callback is async, so import and deletion failures become unhandled rejections. The proposed fixes differ, but the underlying concern of unhandled import failures at that await is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

requestReschedule: deletions are fire-and-forget; failures are now unhandled rejections instead of thrown errors

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) ... })` discards all async callback results. Before this change a synchronous failure in `getCalendar` (e.g. a CalendarService constructor throwing) propagated out of the mutation and produced a visible error; now it, and any dynamic-import rejection, becomes an unhandled promise rejection (a crash risk on Node ≥15). Also, since the callback suspends at `await getCalendar` before calling `deleteEvent`, the calendar/video deletions are not even started before the reschedule email is sent and the mutation returns — if the serverless function is frozen after responding, the old event is never removed from the external calendar/meeting provider even though the booking was already marked cancelled and rescheduled. The loop should be `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (ideally with per-item `.catch` logging) so deletions complete and errors are handled before responding.

getCalendarCredentials now embeds an unawaited Promise in the `calendar` field and discards promises for non-calendar variants

`getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function but now calls the newly-async `getCalendar(credential)` without awaiting it, so the returned objects carry `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` where callers previously received `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` (updated in this PR) awaits that field; any other consumer of this exported helper that touches `item.calendar` synchronously will now operate on a Promise instead of a Calendar and break at runtime, and the `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>` contract changed silently. Additionally, `getCalendar(credential)` is invoked before the `app.variant === "calendar"` check, so for non-calendar-variant apps the promise is created and immediately discarded — a rejection of that dynamic import would be an unhandled rejection. Make the function async, resolve with `Promise.all`, and only call `getCalendar` for credentials that are actually returned.

Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so all apps are still loaded on module evaluation

The object literal evaluates each `import("./applecalendar")` etc. immediately when `packages/app-store/index.ts` is first imported, so every consumer of `@calcom/app-store` still triggers loading all 28 app bundles — just asynchronously instead of synchronously. Any code path that needs a single app (e.g. `getCalendar` for one credential type) pays the module-loading cost for all of them, so the change adds asynchrony without delivering the lazy-loading/startup benefit the PR title implies, and on serverless cold starts everything is still fetched and evaluated. If per-app lazy loading is the goal, store thunks or use lazy getters (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and only invoke the one that is needed.
